2 the warlike: This is an adjective used of Dionysos at OH 30.4 and of the Kouretes’ weapons at OH 38.1 and 7.2 好战的：这是一个形容词，在《俄耳甫斯颂歌》30.4 中用于形容狄俄尼索斯，在《俄耳甫斯颂歌》38.1 和 38.7 中用于形容库雷特斯的武器。
8 into the shape of a savage, dark dragon: The significance of this is obscure. It is probably alluding to some myth now lost to us. Clement cites an anonymous poet referring to the birth of Dionysos from Persephone and Zeus: “A bull, father of a dragon [or: snake], and a father of a bull, a dragon [or: snake]; / in the mountain an oxherd carries his secret goad” (Protrepticus 2.16.3). Note that Demeter’s chariot is drawn by dragons in the following hymn (see OH 40.14+n).8 化身为凶猛的黑暗巨龙：其意义晦涩不明。这很可能是在影射某个现已失传的神话。克莱门特引用了一位匿名诗人的诗句，提及狄俄尼索斯由珀耳塞福涅与宙斯所生：“公牛，巨龙（或：蛇）之父，亦是公牛之父，一条巨龙（或：蛇）；/ 在山中，牧牛人携带着他隐秘的刺棒”（《劝勉篇》2.16.3）。值得注意的是，在接下来的颂歌中，得墨忒耳的战车正是由巨龙牵引（参见《俄耳甫斯颂歌》40.14+注释）。
40. To Eleusinian Demeter40. 致埃琉西斯得墨忒耳
Demeter is the goddess of agriculture, specifically of cereals and their cultivation. She is one of the “original six” Olympians born from Kronos and Rhea. However, as one of the most important fertility goddesses in the Greek pantheon, she often is identified with Earth herself. In antiquity, her name was commonly analyzed as “dē” (believed to have been a variant of “gē,” “earth”) and “mētēr” (“mother”); Orphic fragment 399, for example, addresses her as “Earth mother of all, Demeter, giver of prosperity and wealth.” This identification extends to other fertility goddesses as well, such as Rhea and Kybele (see OH 14i and OH 27i). It is reported that Orpheus himself supposedly claimed Rhea was known as Demeter after the birth of Zeus, etymologizing the “dē” element as related to the “di-” root in Zeus’ name (Orphic fragment 206). Zeus mates with her, and she gives birth to a daughter, Persephone, with whom she is closely connected in cult. We find mention of this already in Hesiod Theogony 912–914. In Orphic accounts of this union, Demeter, here equated with her mother Rhea, attempts to flee the amorous attentions of her son Zeus by transforming herself into a snake. Undeterred, Zeus does likewise, and from this was born Persephone, who has monstrous features that frighten her mother away (see OH 14i). A similar story is found in Arkadia; here, Demeter turns herself into a horse to escape Poseidon, who follows suit. Their children are the Erinyes and the wonder horse Areion (see OH 69i). The ophidian rape by Zeus has been diplomatically omitted from this hymn.得墨忒耳是农业女神，专司谷物及其耕作。她是克洛诺斯与瑞亚所生的"原始六神"之一。然而作为希腊众神谱系中最重要的丰产女神之一，她常被视为大地本身的化身。在古代，她的名字通常被解析为"dē"（被认为是"gē"即"大地"的变体）与"mētēr"（母亲）的组合；例如俄耳甫斯残篇 399 中称她为"万物之母大地，得墨忒耳，繁荣与财富的赐予者"。这种身份认同也延伸至其他丰产女神，如瑞亚与库柏勒（参见 OH 14i 与 OH 27i）。据记载，俄耳甫斯本人曾宣称瑞亚在宙斯诞生后被称为得墨忒耳，并将"dē"的词源与宙斯名字中的"di-"词根相联系（俄耳甫斯残篇 206）。宙斯与她结合，她诞下女儿珀耳塞福涅，二人在祭祀仪式中紧密相连。赫西俄德《神谱》912-914 行已提及此事。在俄耳甫斯传统关于这段结合的叙述中，得墨忒耳（此处等同于其母瑞亚）为躲避儿子宙斯的求爱，将自己变为蛇形试图逃离。 宙斯并未气馁，同样化身为马，由此诞下了珀耳塞福涅，她生有可怖的形貌，吓得母亲远远逃离（参见《俄耳甫斯颂歌》14i）。在阿卡迪亚地区流传着类似的故事：德墨忒尔为躲避波塞冬而化身为马，波塞冬亦随之变形。他们的后代是厄里倪厄斯与神驹阿里翁（参见《俄耳甫斯颂歌》69i）。本颂歌中谨慎地略去了宙斯化蛇侵犯的情节。
The most important myth concerning Demeter is the abduction of Persephone by Hades, memorably told in the beautiful Homeric Hymn to Demeter. The story, however, is not mentioned at all in this hymn but in the following one to Mother Antaia, another name of Demeter, as well as in OH 18, OH 29 and OH 43. For details, see OH 41i. It is notable that again, just as in the case of Zeus’ rape of Demeter, the unpleasantness of the abduction of Persephone is passed over in silence in this hymn.关于德墨忒尔最重要的神话当属哈得斯劫持珀耳塞福涅之事，这在优美的《荷马颂歌·致德墨忒尔》中有令人难忘的叙述。然而本颂歌对此只字未提，相关内容见于后续致安泰娅母亲（德墨忒尔的别称）的颂歌，以及《俄耳甫斯颂歌》第 18、29、43 首。细节可参阅《俄耳甫斯颂歌》41i。值得注意的是，正如对宙斯侵犯德墨忒尔事件的回避，本颂歌同样对珀耳塞福涅被劫持的不快经历保持了沉默。
The account of Persephone’s abduction, Demeter’s search for her, and their consequent reunion formed the foundation myth of the Eleusinian Mysteries, which were very old, perhaps performed in some form as far back as the bronze age. Eleusis is a village that was originally independent of Athens but eventually became part of its territory at some point before the seventh century. The cult was appropriated by the Athenians, who in later times worked hard to give these local mysteries Panhellenic importance, much like Delphi. In this they were quite successful. The mysteries were very popular and continued unabated until officially shut down by the emperor Theodosius in 392 AD, although they were by then already largely neglected. For details of the cult, see Burkert 1985, pp. 285–290, and Larson 2007, pp. 69–85, who also discusses other cults of Demeter and Persephone. The Eleusinian Mysteries were concerned with securing wealth and happiness in this life and a better fate in the hereafter—concerns which we find also in Dionysian/Orphic mysteries, among others, as well. Our hymn focuses exclusively on the material benefits of this life, and it radiates a joy in the wealth and abundance of the world, which may help to explain the omissions of the unsavory mythological elements as noted above. The Eleusinian Mysteries might also be specifically mentioned in our collection because they were felt to have special connection with the actual cult in which the Hymns were in use. It is notable that Mousaios had connections with the Mysteries; see OH Oi. Their prestige might also be a factor in their appearance throughout the collection; compare their possible influence on the early development of the Orphic myth of Dionysos in Graf/Johnston 2007, pp. 73–75. At any rate, the polytheistic nature of Greek religion made such associations possible. One may be a member of many mystery religions, to hedge one’s bets as it were. On one of the Bacchic gold tablets, for example, the initiate claims to “have the rites of Bacchos and Demeter Chthonia and the Mountain Mother” (no. 28). Most likely some, if not all, of our initiates were members in other mystery cults, too.珀耳塞福涅被掳、得墨忒耳寻女以及母女最终团聚的故事构成了厄琉息斯秘仪的基础神话。这一仪式极为古老，可能早在青铜时代就以某种形式存在。厄琉斯村最初独立于雅典，但在公元前七世纪前的某个时期最终并入雅典领土。该秘仪被雅典人吸纳，后来雅典人努力赋予这些地方性秘仪泛希腊化的重要意义，其地位堪比德尔斐。在这方面他们取得了相当大的成功。秘仪曾广受欢迎，其影响力持续不衰，直至公元 392 年被皇帝狄奥多西正式取缔，尽管当时已基本无人问津。关于该秘仪的详细资料，可参阅伯克特 1985 年著作第 285-290 页，以及拉森 2007 年著作第 69-85 页，后者还探讨了得墨忒耳与珀耳塞福涅的其他崇拜形式。厄琉息斯秘仪关注现世的财富与幸福，以及来世更美好的命运——这些关切同样体现在狄俄尼索斯/俄耳甫斯秘仪等其他神秘仪式中。 我们的颂歌专注于今生的物质利益，它散发着对世间财富与丰饶的喜悦，这或许有助于解释为何上文提及的那些令人不悦的神话元素被省略。埃琉西斯秘仪在我们的文集中被特别提及，可能是因为人们认为它们与使用这些颂歌的实际崇拜活动有着特殊联系。值得注意的是，穆赛俄斯与秘仪有所关联；参见《俄耳甫斯颂歌》序言。它们的声望也可能是它们在整个文集中出现的一个因素；比较它们对狄俄尼索斯俄耳甫斯神话早期发展的可能影响，见格拉夫/约翰斯顿 2007 年，第 73-75 页。无论如何，希腊宗教的多神论性质使得这种关联成为可能。一个人可以是多个秘仪的成员，这可以说是一种分散风险的做法。例如，在一块巴克科斯金板上，入会者声称“拥有巴克科斯、冥府得墨忒耳和山母的仪式”（编号 28）。很可能，我们的入会者中，即使不是全部，也有部分人是其他秘仪的成员。
This hymn is the first of a group of four with Eleusinian themes. It comes in the middle of the collection (in terms of number of lines), and it leads directly to the ritual complex involving Dionysos (see OH 44i), which probably was the high point of the rite during which these hymns were originally performed. It is perhaps not accidental that Eleusinian Demeter receives the most elaborate request at the end of her hymn: peace, law, wealth, and health. A number of hymns before this one mention three of these items in their closing appeals (see OH 15i), and the only hymns that mention even two of these afterward are OH 65 and OH 84.这首颂歌是四首以埃琉西斯为主题作品中的第一首。它在整部诗集中（就诗行数量而言）居于中间位置，并直接引向涉及狄俄尼索斯的仪式复合体（参见《俄耳甫斯颂歌》44i 注释），这很可能是最初吟唱这些颂歌时仪式的高潮所在。埃琉西斯的得墨忒耳在其颂歌结尾处获得最详尽的祈求——和平、律法、财富与健康——或许并非偶然。在此之前的若干首颂歌已在结尾祷词中提及其中三项（参见《俄耳甫斯颂歌》15i 注释），而此后仅提及其中两项的颂歌唯有《俄耳甫斯颂歌》65 与 84。
1 Deo: This name of Demeter is usually understood by modern scholars to be a shortened form of “Demeter,” although it is possible that it is just a by-form of the “dē” element. Ancient scholars saw it as such and tried to attach it to words that alluded to aspects of her mythology. For example, the author of the Derveni papyrus, in his interpretation of a poem by Orpheus, asserts that the “dē” is derived from a Greek verb meaning “to tear, to cut up” and explains that Zeus injured the goddess during intercourse, something which he reports that Orpheus “makes clear” later in the poem he was reading (see Betegh 2004, pp. 189–190; the Derveni author might be giving an allegorical meaning to an explicit mention of plowing).1 得俄：德墨忒尔的这一名称通常被现代学者理解为“德墨忒尔”的缩写形式，尽管它可能只是“dē”元素的一种变体。古代学者也持此观点，并试图将其与涉及她神话某些方面的词语联系起来。例如，德尔维尼纸莎草的作者在解读俄耳甫斯的一首诗时断言，“dē”源自一个意为“撕裂、切碎”的希腊语动词，并解释说宙斯在交媾中伤害了这位女神，他报告说俄耳甫斯在他所读的诗的后面部分“明确”指出了这一点（见贝特格 2004 年，第 189-190 页；德尔维尼作者可能是在给一个明确提及耕种的描述赋予寓言意义）。
2 nurturer of youths: This epithet is applied to other divinities in our collection: Hekate (OH 1.8), Artemis (OH 36.8), and Eirene (Peace) in the hymn to Ares (OH 65.9; cf. OH 12.8 and OH 19.22). As the hymn to Ares makes clear, peace and agriculture are closely linked, for when there is no war, men turn their swords to ploughshares; compare lines 4 and 19 of this hymn. Demeter may also be seen as a nurturer of youths insofar as she was nurse to Demophoön and tried to make him immortal (Homeric Hymn to Demeter 2.98–255). This same epithet recurs in line 13.2 青年的养育者：这一称号也用于我们文集中其他神祇：赫卡忒（《俄耳甫斯颂歌》1.8）、阿尔忒弥斯（《俄耳甫斯颂歌》36.8）以及阿瑞斯颂歌中的和平女神厄瑞涅（《俄耳甫斯颂歌》65.9；参见《俄耳甫斯颂歌》12.8 和 19.22）。正如阿瑞斯颂歌所阐明，和平与农业紧密相连，因为当战争停息，人们便将刀剑铸为犁铧；可对照本颂歌第 4 行与第 19 行。得墨忒耳亦可被视为青年的养育者，因她曾哺育德摩丰并试图赐予他永生（《荷马颂歌·致得墨忒耳》2.98–255）。同一称号在第 13 行再次出现。
8–9: Those who were the first to do something were held in high regard by the ancient Greeks, who did not hesitate to invent such figures and/or give credit to the gods when no historical personage was at hand. Here Demeter is lauded as the first to create crops and the first to develop the technical means to harvest them. In respect to the latter, she fits the pattern of the culture hero, the one whose innovations pave the way for the development and improvement of human civilization; cf. OH 38.6+n and OH 76.7+n, where the Kouretes and the Muses respectively teach mortals the sacred rituals (as does Demeter in the Homeric Hymn to Demeter 2.473–482). The most famous divine culture hero in myth is probably Prometheus (see, for example, Aeschylus Prometheus Bound 436–506, and cf. OH 28i and OH 66i). Demeter is said to have taught the Eleusinian prince Triptolemos the secrets of agriculture, and he in turn traveled the world to teach his fellow man. We find Demeter linked to plowing in Hesiod’s injunction to his brother to pray to Demeter and Chthonian Zeus right before beginning to plow (Works and Days 465–469). Another early connection between the goddess and agricultural technique is found in a Homeric simile where Demeter is shown separating grain from chaff (Iliad 5.499–502). 8-9：古希腊人极为推崇那些开创先河者，当缺乏确切的历史人物时，他们毫不迟疑地虚构此类形象或将功绩归于神明。此处得墨忒耳被赞颂为创造作物的第一人，也是发明收割技术手段的首创者。就后者而言，她符合文化英雄的典型模式——其创新为人类文明的发展与进步铺平道路；参见《俄耳甫斯颂歌》38.6+注及 76.7+注，其中库瑞忒斯与缪斯分别向凡人传授神圣仪轨（正如得墨忒耳在《荷马颂歌·致得墨忒耳》2.473-482 中所为）。神话中最著名的神圣文化英雄当属普罗米修斯（例如参阅埃斯库罗斯《被缚的普罗米修斯》436-506，另见《俄耳甫斯颂歌》28 引言及 66 引言）。据传得墨忒耳曾向厄琉西斯王子特里普托勒摩斯传授农业奥秘，后者继而周游世界教导同胞。赫西俄德在《工作与时日》（465-469 行）中告诫其兄弟开始犁地前应向得墨忒耳与冥府宙斯祈祷，可见得墨忒耳与耕作活动的紧密关联。 女神与农业技术的另一早期关联见于荷马史诗的比喻中，得墨忒耳被描绘为将谷物与糠秕分离（《伊利亚特》5.499–502）。
10 Bromios: Another name for Dionysos; the name means the “roarer” (cf. OH 30.1+n). This god becomes associated with Demeter at Eleusis through Iacchos, who seems to be a personified form of the cry the sacred procession would shout out on their way to Eleusis; see OH 42.4+n.10 布罗米俄斯：狄俄尼索斯的另一名称，意为“咆哮者”（参见《俄耳甫斯颂歌》30.1 注释）。这位神祇通过伊阿科斯与埃琉西斯的得墨忒耳产生关联，伊阿科斯似乎是神圣游行队伍前往埃琉西斯途中呼喊声的人格化形态；参见《俄耳甫斯颂歌》42.4 注释。
11 torch-bearing and pure: Torches are typical staples in the process of celebrating fertility divinities, who often have their festivities celebrated at night, including Dionysian revels (see OH 52i and OH 54.10). They were an important part of the Eleusinian cult, as might be deduced from the title of one of its highest functionaries, the Dadoukhos (a word meaning “torch-bearer”); see OH 42.4n. Demeter carries a torch while fasting and in search of her daughter (Homeric Hymn to Demeter 2.47–50, 59–63), and Artemis-Persephone is called Torch-Bearer” (see OH 36.3n). See further OH 9.3n. Purity is a general concern in Greek religion but especially in matters such as initiations. For example, potential initiates in the Eleusinian Mysteries needed to bathe themselves in the sea along with the pig they were to sacrifice. Both these adjectives, then, are as much descriptive of our initiates as they are of the goddess herself. See also OH 30.4+n.11 持火炬且纯洁：火炬是庆祝生育神祇仪式中的典型元素，这些神祇的庆典常在夜间举行，包括酒神狂欢（参见 OH 52i 和 OH 54.10）。它们是厄琉息斯秘仪的重要组成部分，这一点可以从其最高职能人员之一的头衔“达杜科斯”（意为“持火炬者”）中推断出来；参见 OH 42.4n。得墨忒耳在禁食和寻找女儿时手持火炬（《荷马颂歌·得墨忒耳》2.47–50, 59–63），而阿尔忒弥斯-珀耳塞福涅被称为“持火炬者”（参见 OH 36.3n）。更多细节参见 OH 9.3n。纯洁是希腊宗教中的一个普遍关注点，尤其是在入会仪式等事务中。例如，厄琉息斯秘仪的潜在入会者需要与即将献祭的猪一同在海中沐浴。因此，这两个形容词既描述了我们的入会者，也描述了女神本身。另见 OH 30.4+n。
14: A different kind of yoking than mentioned in line 8. Triptolemos is often portrayed in a winged chariot, bringing the knowledge of Demeter to all (see Boardman 1991, p. 219, Boardman 1975, p. 226, and Boardman 1989, p. 226). The dragons here are symbolic of Demeter’s chthonic connection; compare line 12 where the goddess is addressed as appearing from beneath the earth. Demeter Chthonia (Demeter From Beneath the Earth) was in fact worshipped at Hermione (see Larson 2007, pp. 78–79). The dragons might also have a connection with Korybas, who in the previous hymn was said to have taken the form of a dragon in accordance with “Deo’s thinking” (lines 7–8), an obscure allusion.14：此处提及的驾驭方式与第 8 行所述不同。特里普托勒摩斯常被描绘为乘坐带翼战车，将得墨忒耳的智慧传遍四方（参见 Boardman 1991 年著作第 219 页、Boardman 1975 年著作第 226 页及 Boardman 1989 年著作第 226 页）。文中的龙象征得墨忒耳与冥界的联系；可对照第 12 行中女神被称为"从大地之下显现"的描述。事实上，在赫尔米奥涅地区确实存在对冥界得墨忒耳的崇拜（参见 Larson 2007 年著作第 78-79 页）。这些龙也可能与科律巴斯有关联——在前一首颂诗中，科律巴斯曾依照"得俄的意志"化身为龙（第 7-8 行），这是个晦涩的典故。
15: Demeter is here described in maenadic terms; see OH 1.3n. The throne might be referring to Kybele’s throne (see OH 27.5+9n). The circular movement perhaps symbolizes the revolution of the celestial bodies around the earth (see OH 4.3n).15：此处以酒神狂女般的词汇描述得墨忒耳；参见《俄耳甫斯颂歌》1.3 注释。王座可能指库柏勒的王座（参见《俄耳甫斯颂歌》27.5+9 注释）。循环运动或许象征着天体绕地球运行的轨迹（参见《俄耳甫斯颂歌》4.3 注释）。
16 only daughter … many children: The contrasting juxtaposition is typical of our poet’s style, but the reference here is somewhat puzzling. Persephone is usually her only child in myth, but Demeter sometimes is said to have children beside her. In an early myth, she has as a lover the mortal hero Iasion, with whom she lies in a thrice-plowed field. From this union she gives birth to Ploutos (Wealth; see OH 18i), but Iasion is killed by Zeus (Hesiod Theogony 969–974 and Odyssey 5.125–128; see also Homeric Hymn to Demeter 2.488–489). Herodotos mentions that Aeschylus (in a play now lost to us) made Artemis the daughter of Demeter on the basis of an Egyptian tale (2.156.5–6); the historian, however, is skeptical of this last detail. Kallimakhos says that Hekate was the daughter of Demeter (fragment 466; see Orphic fragment 400). Since Artemis and Hekate eventually are identified as the same goddess, it is possible that both births point to one original account, perhaps Orphic. They both might have already been identified with Persephone, too (see OH 29i). However, in our collection Persephone is explicitly said to be Demeter’s only daughter (OH 29.1–2). It is difficult, though not impossible, to construe “many” to just mean Persephone-Artemis-Hekate and Ploutos. On the other hand, “many children” may be symbolic insofar as Demeter is viewed as a nurturer of children (see lines 2 and 13) or it may be used in the sense that the crops she sends up are “her children.” The attribute “only daughter” is even more puzzling, as she has two sisters, Hestia and Hera, in conventional mythology. But Demeter was equated with Hestia and Hera in early Orphic thought (see OH 14i and Betegh 2004, p. 222), and our composer might have in mind Demeter as the personification of female fertility in these lines; this gains some support from the general description of her powers in line 17 and the “many children” in line 16, if we are to understand this attribute broadly. 16 独生女……众多子女：这种对比并置是我们诗人风格的典型特征，但此处的指涉却有些令人费解。在神话中，珀耳塞福涅通常是得墨忒耳唯一的孩子，但有时得墨忒耳也被说成还有其他子女。在一个早期神话中，她与凡人英雄伊阿西翁相恋，两人在一块犁过三遍的田地里结合。这次结合使她生下了普路托斯（财富之神；参见《俄耳甫斯颂歌》18i），但伊阿西翁被宙斯所杀（赫西俄德《神谱》969–974 和《奥德赛》5.125–128；另见《荷马颂歌·致得墨忒耳》2.488–489）。希罗多德提到，埃斯库罗斯（在一部现已失传的剧作中）根据一个埃及故事，将阿尔忒弥斯设定为得墨忒耳的女儿（2.156.5–6）；然而，这位历史学家对这最后一个细节持怀疑态度。卡利马科斯说赫卡忒是得墨忒耳的女儿（残篇 466；参见俄耳甫斯残篇 400）。由于阿尔忒弥斯和赫卡忒最终被认定为同一位女神，这两种出生说法可能指向同一个原始记载，或许是俄耳甫斯教的。她们俩可能也早已与珀耳塞福涅视为同一（参见《俄耳甫斯颂歌》29i）。然而，在我们的诗集中，珀耳塞福涅被明确说是得墨忒耳唯一的女儿（《俄耳甫斯颂歌》29.1–2）。 将"众多"仅仅解释为珀耳塞福涅-阿尔忒弥斯-赫卡忒和普路托斯是困难的，尽管并非不可能。另一方面，"众多子女"可能具有象征意义，因为得墨忒耳被视为儿童的养育者（参见第 2 行和第 13 行），或者它可能用于表示她带来的庄稼是"她的子女"。"独生女"这一属性则更加令人困惑，因为在传统神话中，她有两个姐妹——赫斯提亚和赫拉。但在早期俄耳甫斯思想中，得墨忒耳被等同于赫斯提亚和赫拉（参见《俄耳甫斯颂歌》14i 及 Betegh 2004, p. 222），而我们的作者在这些诗行中可能将得墨忒耳视为女性生育力的化身；如果我们广义地理解这一属性，那么第 17 行对她力量的一般描述以及第 16 行的"众多子女"为此提供了一些支持。
18–20: The repetitions augment the sense of religious fervor and insistence as the hymn closes with a mighty crescendo. The theme running throughout the hymn, that Demeter is a goddess who brings benefits that contribute to the well-being of both the individual and society, is neatly summarized in these lines. The word “riches” is a translation of the Greek “ploutos,” which alludes to her son Ploutos (see note to line 16 above). Peace and rule of law might be intended as personifications of two of the Seasons, Eirene and Eunomia respectively (see OH 43i), and perhaps health should be personified as well (Hygeia), the addressee of OH 68; see also OH 15.10–11n.18–20：重复的语句增强了宗教热忱与坚持感，随着赞歌以强有力的高潮收尾。贯穿整首赞歌的主题——德墨忒尔是一位为个人与社会福祉带来恩惠的女神——在这些诗行中得到了精炼的概括。“财富”一词是对希腊语“ploutos”的翻译，暗指她的儿子普路托斯（参见上文第 16 行注释）。和平与法治可能被拟人化为两位时序女神，分别是厄瑞涅和欧诺弥亚（参见《俄耳甫斯颂歌》43i），或许健康也应被拟人化为许癸厄亚，即《俄耳甫斯颂歌》68 的受颂者；另见《俄耳甫斯颂歌》15.10–11 注释。
41. To Mother Antaia41. 致安泰娅母亲
Mother Antaia is here another name for Demeter. The mythological complex surrounding the abduction of Persephone, absent in the previous hymn, is the focus of this one. Indeed, one of the remarkable features about the hymn is that more than half of it is narrative, a departure from the usual aggregation of epithets, names, and description.安泰亚母亲在此是德墨忒尔的另一个名字。围绕珀耳塞福涅被劫持的神话复合体，在前一首赞歌中未曾出现，而成为本首赞歌的焦点。事实上，这首赞歌的一个显著特点是，超过一半的内容是叙事性的，这与通常堆砌称号、名称和描述的写法有所不同。
The Homeric Hymn to Demeter contains the most famous version of the myth. Demeter fasts in grief after her daughter’s disappearance, although she does not know yet that Hades has abducted her. Hekate comes to assist her, and they find out from Sun what has happened. Depressed, Demeter wanders the world disguised as an old woman (cf. also OH 74i). She eventually reaches Eleusis and becomes a nurse to Demophoön, the newly born son of the king of Eleusis. The baby becomes a kind of surrogate child for the goddess. The mother one night sees the nurse putting her son in the fire and cries out, not knowing that Demeter had intended to make him immortal. In anger Demeter leaves but not before ordering that a temple be built in her honor and promising to introduce rites in Eleusis later. For now, she keeps apart from the gods and causes a great famine with the intent to wipe out the human race and thus deprive the gods of the sacrifices they so very much crave. Hades is willing to let Persephone return, but she has already tasted of the pomegranate seeds he had given to her. Therefore she cannot remain permanently in the land of the living. For the one part of the year she must remain in the underworld with her husband; during this time Demeter grieves over her daughter and nothing grows. However, during the other two parts of the year, she is reunited with her daughter, and in her joy life flourishes anew. Thus the myth explains the origins of the seasons, which the ancient Greeks generally numbered three (see OH 29i). At the end of the poem, Demeter returns to the plains of Rharion outside of Eleusis. She restores the crops and teaches her mysteries, as she had promised, to the princes of Eleusis. There are a number of allusions to this story that are sequentially spread over a number of hymns in the collection; see OH 43i. For a similar story involving Kybele, see OH 27i. The abduction of Persephone and the wanderings of Demeter were the subject of at least one poem attributed to Orpheus (collected under Orphic fragment 379–402; see Richardson 1974, pp. 77–86, for a discussion of the versions of Orpheus, Mousaios, and Eumolpos). Relevant details are in the notes passim.《荷马颂歌·得墨忒耳》包含了这一神话最著名的版本。得墨忒耳在女儿失踪后悲痛绝食，尽管她尚不知晓是哈迪斯掳走了珀耳塞福涅。赫卡忒前来相助，她们从太阳神处得知了真相。沮丧的得墨忒耳化身老妇在世间游荡（另见《俄耳甫斯颂歌》74i 注释），最终抵达厄琉西斯，成为当地国王新生之子得摩丰的乳母。这个婴孩成了女神某种意义上的替代子女。某夜，王后撞见乳母将儿子放入火中，惊骇呼喊——她不知道得墨忒耳本欲赐予孩子永生。愤怒的得墨忒耳在离开前下令建造供奉她的神庙，并承诺日后将在厄琉西斯创立秘仪。此刻她与众神隔绝，并降下大饥荒，意图灭绝人类以断绝诸神渴求的祭品。哈迪斯同意让珀耳塞福涅返回，但她已尝过他赠与的石榴籽，因此无法永久留在生者之境。 一年之中，她必须有一部分时间与丈夫一同留在地府；在此期间，得墨忒耳为女儿哀伤，万物停止生长。然而，在其余的时间里，她与女儿重聚，喜悦之中生命再度繁盛。因此，这个神话解释了季节的起源，古希腊人通常将其分为三个季节（参见 OH 29i）。在诗的结尾，得墨忒耳回到了厄琉息斯城外的拉里昂平原。她恢复了庄稼，并如她所承诺的那样，将她的秘仪传授给了厄琉息斯的王子们。这一故事中有多处暗示，在诗集的若干颂诗中依次展开；参见 OH 43i。关于涉及库柏勒的类似故事，参见 OH 27i。珀耳塞福涅被劫持和得墨忒耳的流浪至少是归于俄耳甫斯名下的一首诗的主题（收录于俄耳甫斯残篇 379–402；关于俄耳甫斯、穆赛俄斯和欧摩尔波斯版本的讨论，参见 Richardson 1974，第 77–86 页）。相关细节散见于各处的注释中。
1 Antaia: The word is properly an adjective with the base meaning of “opposite” and further specialized senses of “hostile” and “besought with prayers.” As an adjective it is used of Kybele in Apollonios of Rhodes Argonautika 1.1141. Later grammarians say that it was also used as a proper name for Rhea and Hekate. It is therefore not surprising to see Demeter called by this name. Both the negative and positive connotations of the word are probably intended in this hymn. The goddess was once hostile to men; now they shower her with prayers, as this hymn does.1 安泰娅：该词本为形容词，基本含义为"对立"，进一步引申为"敌对的"和"被祈求的"。在罗得岛的阿波罗尼俄斯所著《阿尔戈英雄纪》1.1141 中，该形容词被用于形容库柏勒。后世文法学家指出该词亦曾作为瑞亚与赫卡忒的专有名称。因此得墨忒耳被以此名相称并不令人意外。本颂诗中该词的消极与积极内涵可能皆有体现。这位女神曾与人类为敌；如今人们向她倾注祈愿，正如本颂诗所为。
1–2 mother/of immortal gods and of mortal men: Similarly described are Rhea (OH 14.8–9), Earth (OH 26.1), and Kybele (OH 27.7); see also OH 10.1+n.1–2 不朽神灵与终有一死之人的母亲：瑞亚（《俄耳甫斯教颂诗》14.8–9）、盖亚（《俄耳甫斯教颂诗》26.1）与库柏勒（《俄耳甫斯教颂诗》27.7）亦有类似描述；另见《俄耳甫斯教颂诗》10.1 注释。
4: In the Homeric Hymn to Demeter 2.192–211, after the disguised Demeter agrees to be a nurse for Demophoön, she comes to Eleusis. She stands brooding in the palace until an old woman, Iambe, offers her a stool covered with a white fleece. Demeter sits but says nothing until Iambe tells her jokes that make her laugh. She refuses wine from the queen but asks instead that they make for her a drink made of water, barley-meal, and pennyroyal. It is with this that she breaks her fast. The drink, known as the kukeon, was also imbibed by initiates at the Eleusinian Mysteries. In the Orphic version(s), Iambe does not appear, but instead we find a woman named Baubo, a native Eleusinian, who gets the mourning mother to laugh by exposing her pudenda and who then offers her the kukeon that Demeter had earlier refused (Clement of Alexandria Protrepticus 2.20.3–21.1; Orphic fragment 394–395).4：在《荷马颂歌·得墨忒耳》2.192–211 中，伪装后的得墨忒耳同意成为得摩丰的保姆后，她来到厄琉息斯。她在宫殿中沉思站立，直到一位名叫伊阿姆贝的老妇人递给她一张铺着白色羊毛的凳子。得墨忒耳坐下后一言不发，直到伊阿姆贝讲笑话逗她发笑。她拒绝了王后提供的葡萄酒，转而要求用清水、大麦粉和薄荷为她调制一种饮品。她正是以此打破了斋戒。这种被称为"库克翁"的饮品，也是厄琉西斯秘仪中入会者饮用的圣饮。在俄耳甫斯版本中，伊阿姆贝并未出现，取而代之的是一位名叫鲍波的当地厄琉息斯妇女——她通过暴露自己的阴部使悲伤的母亲发笑，随后献上了得墨忒耳早先拒绝的库克翁（亚历山大的克莱门特《劝勉篇》2.20.3–21.1；俄耳甫斯残篇 394–395）。
5–7: In the Homeric Hymn to Demeter, it is not the goddess but rather Hermes who goes into the underworld to fetch Persephone. Dysaules is the husband to Baubo (see the note to line 4 above). Pausanias reports that the Phliasians claim that he was the brother to Keleos (king of Eleusis in the Homeric Hymn to Demeter), that he came to them after being expelled by an Athenian, and that he taught them the mysteries (2.14.2). Pausanias is skeptical of the story, remarking that Dysaules is not mentioned among the group instructed by Demeter in her Homeric hymn and citing lines 2.474–476, but he admits that Dysaules might have arrived due to some other reason (2.14.3). In the Orphic version, Dysaules’ sons Triptolemos and Eubouleus inform Demeter of the abduction of Persephone, and she teaches them the knowledge of agriculture as a reward (Pausanias 1.14.3). Clement of Alexandria tells us that Triptolemos was a cowherd and Eubouleus a swineherd and that the swine of Eubouleus fell into the earth during the abduction of Persephone (Protrepticus 2.20.2 and 2.17.1; see Orphic fragment 390–391). The latter is adduced to explain the custom in the Thesmophoria, a festival in honor of Demeter and Persephone, of women throwing pigs in a pit and later taking back the rotting corpse (see Larson 2007, p. 70), which would seem to be symbolic of Persephone’s (and Demeter’s?) journey. It is likely that Eubouleus is the one to whom the “innocent child of Dysaules” refers in this hymn. 42. To Mise42. 致密斯
Mise is an obscure goddess who appears to be connected with Demeter and Eleusis. She is mentioned in a poem by Herodas, in which a character sees a girl at a “Descent of Mise,” a cultic context that suggests a journey to the underworld (Mimiamb 1.56). In the lexicon of Hesykhios, she is connected with Meter and said to be invoked in oaths (entry M 1442). The name might appear in an account attributed to Asklepiades of Tragilos (fourth century BC) by Harpocration (see Orphic fragment 391), who says that the Eleusinian pair Dysaules and Baubo had two daughters, Protonoe and Nisa, the latter name possibly a corruption of “Misa,” which would be another form of “Mise.” Two inscriptions have been discovered bearing the name. One was found in the precinct of Demeter in Pergamon, the other on an altar dedicated by a priestess to “Mise Kore” near Pergamon. For a review of the evidence and interpretation, see Ricciardelli 2000, pp. 398–400 and Morand 2001, pp. 169–174. In this hymn, Mise is identified with Dionysos and seems to be a reflection of the female side of the god who elsewhere appears androgynous (see note to line 4). Whether they are considered distinct or the same is difficult to determine. The Eleusinian connection is strong in the beginning portion of the hymn: the epithet “law-giving” in line 1 is also a cultic title of Demeter and Persephone, Iacchos was the name of a god chanted by the sacred procession to Eleusis (see note to line 4), and Eleusis is the first place mentioned in the list found in lines 5–10. 43. To the Seasons43. 致时序女神
The Seasons (Greek Horai), as their name suggests, are the personifications of the seasons. This hymn adopts the Hesiodic genealogy (Theogony 901–903) that makes them the daughters of Zeus and Themis (“established custom” or “law”), and, like their mother, they represent an aspect of the cosmic order (see further OH 79i). For Homer, these divinities are in charge of access to Olympos (Iliad 5.748–751) and in one scene take care of the horses of Hera and Athene when they return (Iliad 8.432–435). The Orphic Rhapsodies follow Hesiod with respect to the birth and names of the Seasons (Orphic fragment 252). Their names mean “law-abiding” (“eunomia”), “justice” (“dike”), and “peace” (“eirene”). Dike has her own hymn (OH 62), Eunomia is the mother of the Graces (OH 60.2), and both Eunomia and Eirene are summoned, though not personified, at the end of the hymn to Eleusinian Demeter (OH 40.19; but see OH 40.18–20n). According to Pausanias (9.35.2), however, at Athens there were only two Seasons worshipped, whose names were Karpo (Fruit) and Thallo (Blossom). The Seasons do not merely embody the seasons but also come to represent youthful feminine beauty as well. They clothe Aphrodite when she emerges from the sea and adorn her with numerous ornaments (Homeric Hymn to Aphrodite 6.5–18), and they crown the newly-fashioned Pandora with a garland of spring flowers (Hesiod Works and Days 74–75). The Seasons are also linked with the myth of Persephone’s abduction and return in our collection. The entire story is scattered over several hymns, but nevertheless the chronological order is maintained; in performing the hymns, the initiates recreate the myth piecemeal. The abduction portion appears in two earlier hymns: the one to Plouton, where there is brief narration (OH 18.12–15), and the one to Persephone (OH 29.14). The next part, Demeter’s search and recovery of her daughter, again with short narration, is told in the hymn to Mother Antaia (OH 41.3–7). Now in this hymn, the cycle is completed. Every year, Persephone’s reappearance in the land of the living heralds the beginning of spring, the season of growth. It is not surprising, then, to see the personifications of spring dancing with her in celebration of the return of life (see also OH 29.9–13); note in particular the “circling dances” and “come forth to the light” in line 8 and that their dancing pleases “Zeus and their mother, giver of fruits” in line 9. “Their mother” refers to Themis, who rejoices that the cosmic order, manifested in the cycle of seasons, is maintained. The idea of renewal is also important to Dionysos, the focus of the previous hymn, both because he is a fertility god himself and also because he was reborn, just like his mother Persephone (albeit metaphorically). In this context, the invocation at the end of the hymn that the goddesses appear to the new initiates has special point. They, too, are being “born again” into a new life (see OH 30i). It also segues into the theme of birth, which had appeared in the earlier hymns of the collection and which will dominate OH 44–55 (see OH 44i).季节也与珀耳塞福涅被掳及归来的神话紧密相连，这一主题贯穿于我们的诗集中。整个故事分散在数首颂歌中，但时间顺序得以保留；在吟唱这些颂歌时，信徒们逐步重现了神话的片段。被掳的部分出现在较早的两首颂歌中：一首献给普路同，其中包含简短的叙述（《俄耳甫斯颂歌》18.12–15），另一首献给珀耳塞福涅（《俄耳甫斯颂歌》29.14）。接下来的部分，即得墨忒耳寻找并迎回女儿的故事，同样以简短叙述的形式，在献给安泰亚母亲的颂歌中讲述（《俄耳甫斯颂歌》41.3–7）。而在这首颂歌中，循环得以圆满。每年，珀耳塞福涅重返生者之地，预示着春天的开始，这是生长的季节。因此，看到春天的化身与她共舞，庆祝生命的回归，并不令人意外（另见《俄耳甫斯颂歌》29.9–13）；尤其值得注意的是第 8 行中的“回旋舞”和“走向光明”，以及第 9 行中她们的舞蹈取悦了“宙斯和她们的果实赐予者母亲”。“她们的母亲”指的是忒弥斯，她为体现季节循环的宇宙秩序得以维持而欢欣。 更新的理念对狄俄尼索斯同样至关重要，这位前一首颂歌的核心神祇不仅是丰饶之神，其自身也经历了重生——正如他的母亲珀耳塞福涅那般（尽管是象征意义上的）。在此背景下，颂歌结尾处祈求女神们向新入教者显现的呼唤便具有特殊意义：这些新入教者同样正"重生"进入新生命（参见《俄耳甫斯颂歌》30i 注释）。这也自然过渡到"诞生"这一主题——该主题既出现在本诗集较早的颂歌中，更将主导《俄耳甫斯颂歌》44 至 55 首（参见《俄耳甫斯颂歌》44i 注释）。
The Fates, too, join the festivities. They do so not only because they are the (half-)sisters of the Seasons (see OH 59i) but also because they have a natural interest in the cosmic order as well. The seasons recur as they are fated to do so. We find the Seasons and Fates linked in cultic contexts. In the precinct of Zeus at Athens, Pausanias saw an unfinished statue of the god with both groups above his head (1.40.4). On the altar at Amyklai they were depicted next to Demeter, Persephone, and Plouton, along with Aphrodite, Athene, and Artemis (Pausanias 3.19.4).命运三女神亦加入这场庆典。她们参与不仅因为她们是时序女神的（同母异父）姐妹（参见《俄耳甫斯颂歌》59i 注释），更源于她们对宇宙秩序与生俱来的关切——四季更迭正是命运既定的循环。我们在祭祀语境中常发现时序女神与命运女神的关联：保萨尼阿斯曾在雅典宙斯圣殿目睹未完成的宙斯雕像，其头顶上方同时雕刻着这两组女神（《希腊志》1.40.4）；在阿米克莱的祭坛上，她们则与得墨忒耳、珀耳塞福涅、普路同以及阿佛洛狄忒、雅典娜、阿尔忒弥斯并肩而立（保萨尼阿斯《希腊志》3.19.4）。
The Graces naturally take part in the dance as well. They are very similar to the Seasons in that they, too, are a plurality of three young women who are paradigmatic of feminine beauty and charm (see OH 60i). They join the Seasons in adorning Pandora (Hesiod Works and Days 73–74). In perhaps one of the most beautiful scenes from ancient Greek literature, both groups dance in a circle with Hebe, Harmonia, and Aphrodite. In their midst Artemis sings. Ares and Hermes play along with them. And all of this is in tune with the glorious music of Apollon as he expertly plays the lyre (Homeric Hymn to Apollon 3.186–206). Our composer has skillfully captured the essence of this joie de vivre and grafted it to a genuine religious awe before the uncanny powers of fertility. It is a fitting coda to the block of four hymns with Eleusinian themes.美惠三女神自然也参与舞蹈。她们与季节女神极为相似，同样是由三位年轻女性组成的群体，是女性美丽与魅力的典范（参见 OH 60i）。她们与季节女神一同为潘多拉梳妆打扮（赫西俄德《工作与时日》73-74）。在古希腊文学最动人的场景之一中，这两组女神与赫柏、哈耳摩尼亚及阿佛洛狄忒携手共舞，围成圆圈。阿尔忒弥斯在她们中间歌唱，阿瑞斯与赫尔墨斯相伴奏乐。这一切都与阿波罗精湛演奏里拉琴时奏响的辉煌乐章和谐共鸣（《荷马颂歌·致阿波罗》3.186-206）。我们的诗人巧妙捕捉了这种生命欢愉的精髓，并将其嫁接到对丰饶神秘力量的虔诚敬畏之中。这组四首以厄琉息斯为主题的颂歌，以此作为终章再合适不过。
44. To Semele44. 致塞墨勒
Semele is one of the daughters of Kadmos, the founder of Thebes. Zeus falls in love with her, and they begin to have an affair. Eventually Semele, sometimes at the instigation of a disguised and jealous Hera, secures an oath from Zeus and then demands that he appear to her as he does to his wife. Thus constrained, Zeus reluctantly complies; he reveals himself to the mortal woman in his full stature as god of thunder and lightning. The resulting fireworks burn Semele to a crisp. Zeus notices that she was pregnant, and he decides to save the unborn child. He sews it up in his thigh, and, once it reaches full maturity, Zeus gives “birth” to his son, Dionysos; see Euripides Bacchae 1–42, Apollodoros 3.4.3, Ovid Metamorphoses 3.257–313, Orphic fragment 328, and OH 48.3+n and OH 50.3+n. Sometimes Dionysos is given to Semele’s sister, Ino, to nurse, and she in turn is further pursued by Hera (see OH 74i); in other versions, baby Dionysos is given to his half-brother Hermes, who hands the child off to the Nymphs in the East to rear (see OH 51i), sometimes with Silenos (see OH 54.1+n). For the nurse Hipta, see OH 49i. Semele is already mentioned as the mother of Dionysos by Homer (Iliad 14.325), by Hesiod (Theogony 940–942), and in the three Homeric hymns to Dionysos (1.21, 7.1, 26.2). An alternate name for her is Thyone (Homeric Hymn to Dionysos 1.21, Sappho fragment 17, Apollodoros 3.5.3). The Orphics offered a different version, namely that Dionysos, sometimes called Zagreus, was the son of Zeus and Persephone (see OH 29i), but some accounts attempt to retain the traditional genealogy; for a reconstruction of how and why this was done, see Graf/Johnston 2007, pp. 74–80. In one of these versions, after Dionysos is killed by the Titans, Athene saves his heart and brings it to Zeus; he promptly cuts it up, makes a little soup out of it, and feeds it to Semele, who then is impregnated and gives birth to Dionysos; see Orphic fragment 314–316 and 327, Proclus Hymn to Athene Polymetis 7.7–15 (translation and commentary in van den Berg 2001, pp. 277 and 287–293), West 1983, pp. 162–163, and Graf/Johnston 2007, p. 78. In our collection, both Semele and Persephone are called the mother of Dionysos, but in one case it is implied that Persephone received Dionysos to rear after he was born (presumably by Semele; see OH 46.6–7+n, and cf. OH 30.2+n).塞墨勒是底比斯建城者卡德摩斯的女儿之一。宙斯爱上了她，两人开始了一段恋情。最终，塞墨勒——有时是在伪装且嫉妒的赫拉怂恿下——从宙斯那里得到了一个誓言，然后要求他以对待妻子的方式向她显现。受此约束，宙斯不情愿地答应了；他以雷电之神的完整形态向这位凡间女子显现。随之而来的烈焰将塞墨勒烧成了灰烬。宙斯发现她当时怀有身孕，决定救下这个未出生的孩子。他将胎儿缝进自己的大腿，待其完全成熟后，宙斯“生下”了他的儿子狄俄尼索斯；参见欧里庇得斯《酒神的伴侣》1–42 行、阿波罗多洛斯《书库》3.4.3、奥维德《变形记》3.257–313 行、俄耳甫斯教残篇 328，以及《俄耳甫斯教祷歌》48.3 注和 50.3 注。有时狄俄尼索斯被交给塞墨勒的妹妹伊诺哺乳，而伊诺随后又遭到赫拉的进一步迫害（参见《俄耳甫斯教祷歌》74 注）；在其他版本中，婴儿狄俄尼索斯被交给他的同父异母兄弟赫尔墨斯，后者又将孩子托付给东方的宁芙抚养（参见《俄耳甫斯教祷歌》51 注），有时与西勒诺斯一同照料（参见《俄耳甫斯教祷歌》54.1 注）。关于乳母希普塔，参见《俄耳甫斯教祷歌》49 注。塞墨勒作为狄俄尼索斯之母的记载早已出现在荷马史诗中（《伊利亚特》14.325），赫西俄德（《神谱》940–942），以及三首荷马颂歌献给狄俄尼索斯（1.21, 7.1, 26.2）。她的另一个名字是提俄涅（荷马颂歌献给狄俄尼索斯 1.21，萨福残篇 17，阿波罗多洛斯 3.5.3）。俄耳甫斯教派提供了一个不同的版本，即狄俄尼索斯（有时被称为扎格柔斯）是宙斯和珀耳塞福涅的儿子（见 OH 29i），但一些叙述试图保留传统的谱系；关于如何以及为何这样做的重建，参见 Graf/Johnston 2007，第 74–80 页。在这些版本之一中，狄俄尼索斯被提坦杀死后，雅典娜救了他的心脏并带给宙斯；宙斯迅速将其切碎，用它做了一小碗汤，喂给塞墨勒，后者随后受孕并生下了狄俄尼索斯；见俄耳甫斯残篇 314–316 和 327，普罗克洛斯《献给多谋的雅典娜的颂歌》7.7–15（翻译和注释见 van den Berg 2001，第 277 页和第 287–293 页），West 1983，第 162–163 页，以及 Graf/Johnston 2007，第 78 页。在我们的文集中，塞墨勒和珀耳塞福涅都被称为狄俄尼索斯的母亲，但在一种情况下暗示珀耳塞福涅在狄俄尼索斯出生后（推测由塞墨勒所生）接收并抚养了他（见 OH 46.6–7+n，并比较 OH 30.2+n）。
This hymn begins a series (through OH 54) whose focus is on Dionysos; in particular, these hymns are linked by the motif of (re)birth, a theme that is prevalent at the beginning of the collection (see OH 2i). A number of them refer to ritual contexts and, insofar as the hymns are performative acts (see OH 30i), probably reflect something of the actual activities of our cult during this particular rite, though details are vague; see lines 6–9 and note.这首颂歌开启了一个以狄俄尼索斯为核心的系列（直至《俄耳甫斯颂歌》第 54 首）；特别是，这些颂歌通过（重）生的母题相互关联，这一主题在诗集开篇部分尤为突出（参见《俄耳甫斯颂歌》第 2 首引言）。其中多首提及仪式场景，且鉴于这些颂歌本身具有仪式表演性（参见《俄耳甫斯颂歌》第 30 首引言），很可能反映了我们教团在此特定仪式中的实际活动，尽管细节模糊；参见第 6-9 行及注释。

6–9: There is a tradition that Dionysos descended into the underworld to retrieve his mother and convey her to Olympos (Pausanias 2.37.5; cf. Pindar Olympian Odes 2.25–28 and the comic parody in Aristophanes Frogs, in which Dionysos goes to fetch the recently-departed playwright Euripides). Here, though, it seems that Persephone has received her kindly in the underworld. Semele might originally have been an earth goddess, and these lines might be an indirect remnant of this tradition. The “ritual of the table” is obscure. Perhaps it is related to the myth mentioned in the introduction to the hymn that has Zeus feeding Semele Dionysos-soup. Note the phrase “all mortal men reenact your travail,” which of course suggests birth, and it would certainly be easier for a worshipper to drink soup in a ritual context than to be set on fire (see also OH 47.5n). 45. Hymn to Dionysos Bassareus and Triennial45. 致巴萨瑞乌斯与三年节狄俄尼索斯颂歌

OH 52, which is addressed to Triennial and which mentions Bassaros in line 12, a variant of Bassareus. This epithet is derived from the Thracian word “bassara,” “fox” and, by extension, the fox-skin worn at times by the god and his maenads. Thracian maenads could be called Bassarids, and a lost play by Aeschylus bears their name as a title. In this play, it seems they tear apart Orpheus, who, incidentally, is their countryman. The violence mentioned in our hymn might very well have been influenced by this play, although by now the violent death of Orpheus had become a literary standard. In any case, it is possible that the Thracian connection induced our poet to include a hymn addressed to Dionysos Bassareus. Bassarids are first mentioned by Anakreon (PMG 411b), who also uses a related verb, “anabassareō,” to indicate reveling at a symposium (PMG 356a). This hymn continues the birth theme (see OH 44i) and alludes to maenadic ritual in lines 3–5. It is not difficult to conceive a period of joyous shouting, dancing, and brandishing of thyrsi (perhaps limited to the female initiates, if there were any) that was intended to be symbolic at the rite when this hymn was performed; see also OH 52i and OH 54i.狄俄尼索斯已是《俄耳甫斯颂歌》第 30 首的献祭对象，但本颂歌是献给狄俄尼索斯特定祭祀身份系列中的首篇。此处他被唤作巴萨柔斯与三年节之神；参见《俄耳甫斯颂歌》第 52 首——该颂歌献给三年节之神，并在第 12 行提及巴萨柔斯的变体"巴萨罗斯"。这一称号源自色雷斯语"巴萨拉"，意为"狐狸"，进而引申指代该神及其迈那得斯女信徒时而披戴的狐皮。色雷斯的迈那得斯可被称为巴萨里得斯，埃斯库罗斯一部失传的剧作便以其名为题。该剧中，她们似乎撕裂了同为色雷斯人的俄耳甫斯。本颂歌提及的暴力场景很可能受此剧影响，尽管俄耳甫斯惨死的情节在当时已成为文学经典。无论如何，可能是色雷斯元素的关联促使诗人将这首献给狄俄尼索斯·巴萨柔斯的颂歌纳入诗集。巴萨里得斯最早见于阿那克里翁的记载（《希腊诗选》411b），他同时使用相关动词"阿纳巴萨雷奥"来指研讨会中的狂欢（《希腊诗选》356a）。本颂歌延续了诞生主题（参见《俄耳甫斯颂歌》44i 引言），并在第 3-5 行隐晦地指向迈那得斯仪式。 不难想象，在吟唱这首颂歌的仪式上，曾有过一段充满欢欣呼喊、舞蹈与挥舞酒神杖（或许仅限于女性入会者，如果当时存在的话）的时期，这旨在象征仪式意义；另见 OH 52i 与 OH 54i。

In the context of discussing initiation, Plato gives a prose quotation vaguely attributed to “the followers of the mysteries” that “the fennel-stalk bearers [narthēkophoroi] are many, the bacchoi few” (Phaedo 69c = Orphic fragment 576), which seems to point to a distinction between general worship of Dionysos (maenadism?) and the more restricted mystery cults that require initiation, such as the Eleusinian Mysteries (see also Graf/Johnston 2007, p. 143). The thyrsos is sometimes used as a weapon, e.g., by Dionysos in the Gigantomachy or by a maenad repelling the licentious advances of a satyr in vase paintings (e.g., Boardman 1975, pl. 313). See also OH 44.3, OH 50.8, and OH 52.4.5 酒神杖：酒神杖是一种顶端饰有松果的魔杖，有时缠绕着常春藤。杖杆可由茴香茎制成；参见《俄耳甫斯颂歌》42.1 及欧里庇得斯《酒神的伴侣》147 行。这是狄俄尼索斯崇拜中最普遍的象征物之一，文献中频繁提及，图像中也常有描绘。在讨论入会仪式的语境中，柏拉图曾引用一段模糊归因于“秘仪追随者”的散文：“持茴香杖者众多，酒神信徒寥寥”（《斐多篇》69c = 俄耳甫斯残篇 576），这似乎指向了普通狄俄尼索斯崇拜（狂女仪式？）与需要入会仪式的更严格秘仪（如厄琉息斯秘仪）之间的区别（另见 Graf/Johnston 2007, p. 143）。酒神杖有时被用作武器，例如在巨人之战中由狄俄尼索斯使用，或在瓶画中由狂女击退萨提尔的淫秽进犯（如 Boardman 1975, pl. 313）。另见《俄耳甫斯颂歌》44.3、50.8 及 52.4。
5 wrathful in the extreme: Examples of Dionysos’ wrath abound in mythology, particularly in a group of myths that involve the rejection of his worship. Some of the more famous victims include Lykourgos, the Thracian king who hounded Dionysos and his maenads (Iliad 6.130–140), Pentheus and the women of Thebes (Euripides Bacchae), the daughters of Minyas, who eschewed going to the mountains to worship the god (Ovid Metamorphoses 4.1–40 and 390–415; also see the Plutarch citation in note to line 3), and the daughters of Proitos, who in some versions of their story also refuse Dionysos (Apollodoros 2.2.2). Orpheus himself experienced the god’s wrath after rejecting him, being ripped apart (sparagmos) by maenads and/or the Bassarids (see OH 52i). See also OH 30.4+n and OH 47i.5 极端愤怒：狄俄尼索斯的愤怒在神话中比比皆是，尤其体现在一系列拒绝崇拜他的神话中。一些较为著名的受害者包括色雷斯国王吕库尔戈斯，他曾追捕狄俄尼索斯及其狂女（《伊利亚特》6.130–140）；忒拜的彭透斯与妇女们（欧里庇得斯《酒神的伴侣》）；米尼亚斯的女儿们，她们拒绝上山敬拜这位神祇（奥维德《变形记》4.1–40 及 390–415；另见第 3 行注释中引用的普鲁塔克记载）；以及普罗伊托斯的女儿们，在某些版本的故事中她们也拒绝了狄俄尼索斯（阿波罗多洛斯 2.2.2）。俄耳甫斯本人在拒绝这位神祇后亦亲历其怒，被狂女和/或巴萨里德们撕成碎片（肢解）（参见 OH 52i）。另见 OH 30.4+n 及 OH 47i。
7 leaping god: Leaping, frolicking, gamboling, prancing—all these are typical expressions of abandon in ecstatic cult; Dionysos himself often leads the wild processionals (see, e.g., OH 52.3–4 and 7–8). Other related figures described in similar terms are Pan (OH 11.4), the Nereids (OH 24.7), the Kouretes (OH 31.1), and the Nymphs with Pan (OH 51.8). Note that all of these are groups, save Pan, who, like Dionysos, can function as chorus-leader. The leaping may have fertility connotations like the “leaping” in the Palaikastro hymn to Zeus does (see OH 31i). Dionysos is called the “dancer” at OH O.8, and his “feet quiver in the dance” at OH 46.4.7 跳跃之神：跳跃、嬉戏、欢腾、雀跃——这些都是狂喜崇拜中典型的放纵表达；狄俄尼索斯本人常引领狂野的游行队伍（参见例如《俄耳甫斯颂歌》52.3–4 和 7–8）。其他以类似方式描述的相关形象包括潘神（《俄耳甫斯颂歌》11.4）、涅瑞伊得斯（《俄耳甫斯颂歌》24.7）、库瑞忒斯（《俄耳甫斯颂歌》31.1）以及潘神与宁芙们（《俄耳甫斯颂歌》51.8）。值得注意的是，除潘神外，这些均为群体形象，而潘神与狄俄尼索斯相似，都能担任合唱领队。这种跳跃可能具有生育寓意，正如帕莱卡斯特罗献给宙斯的颂歌中的“跳跃”所体现的（参见《俄耳甫斯颂歌》31i）。狄俄尼索斯在《俄耳甫斯颂歌》O.8 中被称为“舞者”，在《俄耳甫斯颂歌》46.4 中则描述其“双足在舞蹈中颤动”。
46. To Liknites46. 致利克尼特斯
This hymn is addressed to Dionysos Liknites (Dionysos of the cradle), who is also mentioned in OH 52.3. The title “Liknites” comes from the Greek word “liknon,” the primary meaning of which is “winnowing-fan.” This was a common cult object in Dionysian mysteries, well-attested in vase paintings (e.g., Boardman 1989, pl. 233) and often containing a phallus; see Graf/Johnston 2007, p. 148, and compare the story of Korybas’ murder (OH 39i). There are hints in later writers of a story in which the goddess Hipta places a winnowing fan on her head, wreathes it with a snake, and receives the infant Dionysos in it after he is born from Zeus’ thigh (Orphic fragment 329); this coheres with her role as nurse of Dionysos in our collection (see OH 49.1). An enigmatic vase painting from the Classical period might be depicting a variant of this account (Boardman 1989, pl. 157; for discussion, see Loucas 1992); here, a woman (Hipta?) is bearing a covered winnowing-basket to two seated gods, who might be Sabazios and Kybele (see also OH 49i).这首颂歌献给狄俄尼索斯·利克尼特斯（摇篮中的狄俄尼索斯），在《俄耳甫斯颂歌》第 52.3 节中亦有提及。"利克尼特斯"这一称号源于希腊语"liknon"，其本意为"扬谷扇"。此物乃狄俄尼索斯秘仪中常见的祭祀法器，在瓶画中多有印证（如博德曼 1989 年图版 233），常内置阳具形象；参见格拉夫/约翰斯顿 2007 年第 148 页，并可对照科律巴斯谋杀案传说（《俄耳甫斯颂歌》第 39 节注）。后世文献隐现一则传说：女神希普塔将扬谷扇顶于首，以蛇缠绕其周，在狄俄尼索斯自宙斯大腿诞生后以此器承接婴孩（俄耳甫斯残篇 329）；此说与其在我们辑录中担任狄俄尼索斯乳母的职责相契合（参见《俄耳甫斯颂歌》第 49.1 节）。一幅古典时期的神秘瓶画或为此传说的变体（博德曼 1989 年图版 157；相关论述见卢卡斯 1992 年）：画中女子（希普塔？）正将覆有罩布的扬谷篮呈递给两位端坐神祇，二者可能是萨巴奇奥斯与库柏勒（另见《俄耳甫斯颂歌》第 49 节注）。
Dionysos was worshipped as Liknites at Delphi, and Plutarch tells us that it was believed his remains had been brought there (De Iside et Osiride 365a). This dovetails with one version of the Orphic myth of the Titans’ dismemberment of Dionysos where it is Apollon who gathers the remains of his half-brother and buries them on Parnassos (Orphic fragment 322). Plutarch further says that the Holy Ones perform a secret sacrifice in Apollon’s temple when Liknites is awakened by the Thyiads, a group of Attic women who performed maenadic rituals for Dionysos every other year on the slopes of Parnassos (see OH 52i and OH 53i; see further Plutarch Mulierum virtutes 249e–f and De primo frigido 953d). Dionysos was the most important deity at Delphi for three months in the winter, when Apollon was thought to be vacationing up north among the Hyperboreans. There is also some obscure testimony that Dionysos was at Delphi before Apollon, perhaps even identified with Python, the serpent Apollon kills (for Python, see OH 34.3n; for the identification of Dionysos and Python, see Fontenrose 1959, pp. 374–379). For more information on the worship of Dionysos at Delphi, see West 1983, pp. 150–152, and Larson 2007, pp. 137–138; cf. also OH 79.7–10n. Our hymn does not appear to refer explicitly to the Delphic Liknites, but for the sleeping Dionysos, see OH 53.2–3+i. The theme of birth continues in this hymn. It also adds the notion of vegetation (“blossoming” in line 2), which is further developed in some of the following hymns, thus highlighting Dionysos’ connection with plant-life (see further OH 50i). There is no explicit mention of a ritual, but the name itself implies one, and it can easily be imagined that at this stage of the rite a winnowing-basket was brought in and/or its contents revealed (see OH 47i).狄奥尼索斯在德尔斐被尊奉为利克尼特斯，普鲁塔克告诉我们，人们相信他的遗骸被带到了那里（《论伊西斯与奥西里斯》365a）。这与俄耳甫斯神话中泰坦肢解狄奥尼索斯的一个版本相吻合，其中阿波罗收集了他同父异母兄弟的遗骸，并将它们埋葬在帕纳索斯山上（俄耳甫斯残篇 322）。普鲁塔克进一步说，当利克尼特斯被提亚德斯唤醒时，圣徒们在阿波罗的神殿中进行秘密祭祀；提亚德斯是一群阿提卡妇女，她们每隔一年在帕纳索斯山坡上为狄奥尼索斯举行酒神仪式（参见 OH 52i 和 OH 53i；另见普鲁塔克《论妇女的美德》249e–f 和《论初寒》953d）。在冬季的三个月中，狄奥尼索斯是德尔斐最重要的神祇，那时人们认为阿波罗正在北方的许珀耳玻瑞亚人中度假。还有一些晦涩的证词表明，狄奥尼索斯在阿波罗之前就在德尔斐，甚至可能与阿波罗杀死的巨蟒皮同相提并论（关于皮同，参见 OH 34.3n；关于狄奥尼索斯与皮同的同一性，参见 Fontenrose 1959，第 374–379 页）。有关德尔斐对狄奥尼索斯崇拜的更多信息，参见 West 1983，第——页。 150–152 页，以及拉森 2007 年，第 137–138 页；另参见 OH 79.7–10 注释。我们的颂歌似乎并未明确提及德尔斐的利克尼特斯，但关于沉睡的狄俄尼索斯，请参见 OH 53.2–3+注释。本颂歌延续了出生的主题，并引入了植被的概念（第 2 行中的“绽放”），这一概念在后续的一些颂歌中得到了进一步发展，从而突显了狄俄尼索斯与植物生命的联系（详见 OH 50 注释）。虽然未明确提及仪式，但名称本身暗示了仪式的存在，可以轻易想象，在仪式的这一阶段，会引入一个簸箕并/或展示其内容物（参见 OH 47 注释）。
2–3: The Nymphs rear Dionysos already in Homer (Iliad 6.132) and are found throughout the collection in this capacity (see OH 30.8n). Apollonios of Rhodes recounts that a specific nymph, Makris, received the infant Dionysos (Argonautika 4.540 and 1131–1140). For other nurslings of nymphs, see OH 51.3n. Hipta, too, is called the “nurse of Bacchos” (OH 49.1), while sometimes it is his aunt Ino, among others, who rears the child after her sister perishes (see OH 44i). Nysa is the name of a number of mountains in Asia Minor, and it is where Dionysos is often said to have been reared by the Nymphs; see the two shorter Homeric hymns to Dionysos (1.6–9, where Nysa is situated in Egypt [cf. Herodotos 2.146.2]) and 26.3–9, as well as Apollodoros 3.4.3 and OH 51.15. Its appearance here stresses Dionysos’ Eastern associations, as do Sabazios and Hipta, the addressees of the two hymns after the next, respectively; note, too, that a winnowing basket seems to have been a part of Sabazios’ mysteries, at least in Athens (see OH 48i). In ancient etymologies Nysa was used to explain Dionysos’ name (for a somewhat technical discussion, see West 1978, pp. 373–375, with further references). The Homeric Hymn to Demeter locates the abduction of Persephone in the Nysian field (2.17) but gives no indication where this field might be in the world. The mention of Aphrodite suggests an identification with Adonis; see further note to lines 6–7. 2-3：在荷马史诗中，宁芙们已开始抚养狄俄尼索斯（《伊利亚特》6.132），且整部诗集中她们常以此身份出现（参见《俄耳甫斯颂歌》30.8 注）。罗德岛的阿波罗尼奥斯记载，一位名为玛克里斯的宁芙曾收留婴儿狄俄尼索斯（《阿尔戈英雄纪》4.540 及 1131-1140）。关于宁芙抚养的其他神祇，参见《俄耳甫斯颂歌》51.3 注。希普塔亦被称为“巴克斯的乳母”（《俄耳甫斯颂歌》49.1），而有时抚养这孩子的则是其姨母伊诺等人——在其生母亡故之后（参见《俄耳甫斯颂歌》44i 注）。尼萨是小亚细亚数座山脉的名称，传说狄俄尼索斯常在此由宁芙们抚养长大；参见两篇较短的荷马式狄俄尼索斯颂诗（1.6-9，其中尼萨位于埃及[对照希罗多德《历史》2.146.2]）及 26.3-9，另见阿波罗多洛斯《书库》3.4.3 与《俄耳甫斯颂歌》51.15。此处提及尼萨意在强调狄俄尼索斯与东方的关联，紧随其后两篇颂歌的献祭对象——萨巴奇俄斯与希普塔——亦具此意；需注意，扬谷篮似为萨巴奇俄斯秘仪的一部分，至少在雅典如此（参见《俄耳甫斯颂歌》48i 注）。古代词源学中，“尼萨”常被用以阐释狄俄尼索斯之名（相关学术讨论参见韦斯特 1978 年著作第 373-375 页及其引述文献）。 《荷马颂歌·德墨忒尔篇》将珀耳塞福涅的劫持地点定于尼西安田野（2.17），但未指明该田野位于世间何处。提及阿芙洛狄忒暗示其与阿多尼斯的关联；详见第 6-7 行注释。
4 quiver in the dance: For Dionysos as a dancing god, see OH 45.7n and OH 52i.4 舞动时颤抖：关于狄俄尼索斯作为舞蹈之神，参见《俄耳甫斯颂歌》45.7 注及 52 首引言。
5: Compare the short Homeric Hymn to Dionysos (no. 26) and see OH 51.15–16n.5：可对照简短的《荷马颂歌·狄俄尼索斯篇》（第 26 首），参见《俄耳甫斯颂歌》51.15-16 注。
6–7: Persephone is often the mother of Dionysos in Orphic mythology, but here she is the ultimate nurse of the child Dionysos, just as she is the nurse of Aprhodite’s son Adonis (compare line 3 and see OH 56i). This would seem to contradict other hymns in the collection where she is explicitly the mother of Dionysos (e.g., OH 30.6–7), and it is possible that we have a vague reference to a tradition that retained Semele as the conventional mother of Dionysos and worked in Persephone as his most important nurse. For the problem of reconciling the birth of Dionysos from both Semele and Persephone in Orphism, see OH 30.2n and OH 44i.6-7：在俄耳甫斯神话中，珀耳塞福涅常被视作狄俄尼索斯之母，但此处她是幼年狄俄尼索斯的终极哺育者，正如她也是阿芙洛狄忒之子阿多尼斯的哺育者（对照第 3 行并参见《俄耳甫斯颂歌》56 首引言）。这似乎与本诗集其他明确将珀耳塞福涅列为狄俄尼索斯之母的颂歌相矛盾（如《俄耳甫斯颂歌》30.6-7），可能此处模糊指涉了某种保留塞墨勒作为狄俄尼索斯传统母亲、同时将珀耳塞福涅塑造为其最重要哺育者的传说传统。关于俄耳甫斯教中调和狄俄尼索斯同时出自塞墨勒与珀耳塞福涅的难题，参见《俄耳甫斯颂歌》30.2 注及 44 首引言。
7 loved by the deathless gods: The manuscripts have “feared” instead of “loved,” which is odd since Dionysos quickly became an accepted member of the Olympic pantheon (e.g., for fetching Hephaistos; see OH 66i). If “feared” should be retained, perhaps comparable is Alexander’s mother, Olympias, who scared men with tamed snakes coming out of winnowing-baskets (Plutarch Alexander 2.9); compare Pan’s birth (OH 11i). On the other hand, this idea of fear might just be a generic reference to the kind of horror Dionysos can effect (as at the end of Euripides’ Bacchae); compare the “bloody swords” and “wrathful to the extreme” in OH 45.3 and 5.7 为不朽众神所爱：手稿中写的是“畏惧”而非“爱”，这颇为奇怪，因为狄俄尼索斯迅速成为了奥林匹斯众神中备受接纳的一员（例如，他曾带回赫菲斯托斯；参见《俄耳甫斯颂歌》66i）。若应保留“畏惧”一词，或许可类比亚历山大大帝的母亲奥林匹亚斯，她曾用从簸箕中爬出的驯服蛇吓唬众人（普鲁塔克《亚历山大传》2.9）；亦可参照潘神的诞生（《俄耳甫斯颂歌》11i）。另一方面，这种恐惧的观念或许只是泛指狄俄尼索斯所能引发的恐怖（如欧里庇得斯《酒神的伴侣》结尾处）；比较《俄耳甫斯颂歌》45.3 与 5 中提到的“血染的剑”与“极端愤怒”。
47. To Perikionios47. 致佩里基奥尼奥斯
This hymn, like the previous one, is addressed to Dionysos in one of his particular ritual manifestations, albeit one rather obscure to us. “Perikionios” means “twined round the pillar,” and the only reference to this title comes from a scholiast to Euripides Phoenician Women 651, who cites the late third- or early second-century historian Mnaseas (fragment 18). The brief notice states that after the palace of Kadmos had been blasted by Zeus’ lightning, ivy enveloped it to protect the infant therein; thus Dionysos was called Perikionios among the Thebans. Our poet might very well have had something like this in mind, especially if it is Dionysos who causes the ivy to cover the palace in the original myth (cf. line 2). It is possible that some confusion has occurred; our composer might have been influenced inadvertently by the story of Dionysos and the pirates, where as part of his epiphany ivy covers the sail and mast of their ship (Homeric Hymn to Dionysos 7.38–42). The far distance of our cult from Thebes could have facilitated such a misunderstanding. Perhaps related is Pausanias’ account of the Thebans’ claim that after Semele had been struck by the thunderbolt, a log fell down from heaven and that subsequently a certain Polydoros (Semele’s brother in some sources) decked it out in bronze and called it Dionysos Kadmeios (9.12.3). This is Theban cult, but a number of Athenain vase paintings show a pole or column outdoors on which is affixed a mask of Dionysos (bearded) with other accoutrements (e.g., Boardman 1989, pl. 24). There are scenes of women around it handling wine or dancing wildly (sometimes with satyrs); see Larson 2007, p. 135. One in particular might have some (albeit indirect) relevance for our collection. On one side the mask of Dionysos lies in a liknon among ivy with two women standing around, one carrying a basket of fruit, the other a wine decanter (see Boardman 1989, pl. 233). This probably represents the stage before the mask is ritually affixed to the column. It is perhaps not a coincidence, then, that this hymn follows the one addressed to Dionysos Liknites and part of the rite performed by our initiates might have consisted of a mask of Dionysos being carried to a column, accompanied by the initiates’ singing the previous hymn to Liknites, and then the incense offering being given as this hymn was sung. That is not to say that our cult had preserved a centuries-old form of worship unchanged. It is more likely that certain types of Dionysian worship were adopted and adapted in Orphic (and other) circles (compare the notion of the bricoleur in Graf/Johnston 2007, pp. 70–71 and passim; cf. also OH 4i). It is also a possibility that a rite might have been invented or an older one altered in later times on the basis of literary sources (see note to line 5) or under the influence of a local indigenous cult through an identification with a Hellenic divinity. 5: Who is “everyone” and why were they tied up? The hymn seems to refer to a single specific event, and up to this point the one that makes the most sense is the first “birth” of Dionysos at the death of Semele. Imprisonment, however, is not part of that story. Another possibility is suggested by a comparison to Euripides Bacchae. While there is no explicit connection in terms of language, and while Euripides mentions the palace of Pentheus and not Kadmos, nonetheless in the play Dionysos first causes an earthquake and then sets his mother’s grave on fire with lightning bolts (576–603). The latter detail is certainly an explicit allusion to Dionysos’ birth, the legitimacy of which is called in question at the outset of the play. Afterward we find out how Dionysos tricked Pentheus in order to escape his earlier imprisonment (604–641). Our poet seems to have grafted some literary antecedents to the particular ritual act that this hymn accompanies. The vivid details stir the imagination of the participants. In essence, the performance of this hymn recreates a mythic scenario, composed of the birth of Dionysos (compare the ritual of the table mentioned in OH 44.6–9+n) and aspects of his epiphanies found in previous literature. The “everyone” then would be the initiates, and the “bonds” a metaphor for their previous uninitiated life. 48. To Sabazios48. 致萨巴齐俄斯
Sabazios was a Phrygian god. His worship is first attested to have reached Greece by the end of the fifth century. Aristophanes mentions him in a number of contexts. Two guards attribute their sleepiness to him, probably because of intoxication (Wasps 9–10). His mysteries are mentioned in the context of female ecstatic worship (Lysistrata 387–390), and he is mentioned alongside Kybele in a list of gods related to birds (Birds 873–875). One fragment, from the play Seasons, calls him Phrygian and a player of the aulos (fragment 578), an instrument particularly connected to Dionysian ecstatic worship. Demosthenes gives us some insight into the practice of his cult in fourth-century Athens, although we need to take his account with a grain of salt because he is trying to smear his rival Aeschines (18.259–260; see also Orphic fragment 577). While Sabazios is not explicitly named as the god of this cult, the latter is invoked with the cry “euoi, Saboi,” and Strabo explicitly links the cult to Sabazios and Kybele (10.3.18). There are a number of Dionysian elements present: ivy, winnowing-basket (see OH 46.2–3n), fawn-skins, ecstatic dancing and singing. Initiations are mentioned, and one element that stands out is the handling of live snakes (also an element in some Dionysian cults; see also OH 46.7n). Sabazios’ name appears in Orphic contexts, although he is not attested in any of the fragments attributed to Orpheus. He is identified with Dionysos as the son of Zeus and Persephone (Diodorus Siculus 4.4.1), and Clement of Alexandria mentions his mysteries in the context of Zeus mating with Persephone in the form of a snake (Protrepticus 2.16.2). For the possible influence of Sabazios’ worship on this Orphic genealogy, see West, 1983, pp. 97 and 110. However, the importance of Sabazios in Asia Minor also allowed his identification with Zeus, as in our hymn, which retains the Dionysian connection by making Sabazios the father of Dionysos (but see OH 49.2n); interestingly enough, the historian Mnaseas called Sabazaios the son of Dionysos (fragment 36). Among the four inscriptions dedicated to “mother Hipta,” Sabazios-Zeus is mentioned in three of them (see OH 49i). This hymn fits the birth theme that is prominent in this central Dionysian group (see OH 44i) and, with the following hymn, forms a male-female pairing, a familiar pattern in the collection (see OH 14.8–9n). That two divinities from Phrygia in Asia Minor are given such a prominent position is a strong indication that our cult was also located in this region.萨巴齐奥斯是一位弗里吉亚神祇。其崇拜活动最早可追溯至公元前五世纪末传入希腊。阿里斯托芬在多个语境中提及他：两名守卫将困倦归咎于他（可能因醉酒所致，《马蜂》9-10 行）；在女性狂喜崇拜的语境中提及其秘仪（《吕西斯特拉忒》387-390 行）；在与鸟类相关的神祇名录中他与库柏勒并列（《鸟》873-875 行）。戏剧《季节》的残篇 578 称他为弗里吉亚的奥洛斯笛演奏者——这种乐器尤其与狄俄尼索斯的狂喜崇拜相关。德摩斯梯尼为我们揭示了公元前四世纪雅典对其崇拜的实践，但需谨慎对待其叙述，因其意在抹黑政敌埃斯基涅斯（《演说集》18.259-260；另见俄耳甫斯残篇 577）。虽然未明确记载此崇拜之神名，但仪式中呼喊“欧伊，萨波伊”的祷词，以及斯特拉博明确将该崇拜与萨巴齐奥斯、库柏勒相关联（《地理志》10.3.18），皆指向其身份。该崇拜包含诸多狄俄尼索斯元素：常春藤、扬谷篮（参见《俄耳甫斯颂歌》46.2-3 注释）、幼鹿皮、狂喜的舞蹈与歌唱。 入会仪式被提及，其中一个突出的元素是活蛇的处理（这也是某些狄俄尼索斯教派中的元素；另见 OH 46.7n）。萨巴齐俄斯的名字出现在俄耳甫斯语境中，尽管在归因于俄耳甫斯的任何片段中都没有得到证实。他被认定为狄俄尼索斯，是宙斯与珀耳塞福涅的儿子（狄奥多罗斯·西库卢斯 4.4.1），亚历山大的克莱门特在宙斯以蛇的形式与珀耳塞福涅交配的背景下提到了他的神秘仪式（《劝勉篇》2.16.2）。关于萨巴齐俄斯崇拜对这一俄耳甫斯谱系的可能影响，参见 West，1983 年，第 97 页和 110 页。然而，萨巴齐俄斯在小亚细亚的重要性也使他与宙斯等同，正如我们的赞歌中所保留的那样，通过将萨巴齐俄斯视为狄俄尼索斯的父亲来保持与狄俄尼索斯的联系（但参见 OH 49.2n）；有趣的是，历史学家姆纳塞亚斯称萨巴扎俄斯为狄俄尼索斯的儿子（片段 36）。在献给“母亲希普塔”的四篇铭文中，有三篇提到了萨巴齐俄斯-宙斯（见 OH 49i）。 这首颂歌契合了狄俄尼索斯核心群体中突出的诞生主题（见 OH 44i），并与下一首颂歌形成男女配对的模式，这是本诗集中常见的结构（参见 OH 14.8–9n）。两位来自小亚细亚弗里吉亚的神祇被赋予如此突出的地位，强烈暗示了我们的崇拜仪式也位于这一地区。

49. To Hipta49. 致希普塔
Hipta was an Asiatic mother goddess of whom very little is known. Proclus mentions her in connection with the Orphic version of Dionysos’ birth from Zeus’ thigh: she receives the child in a winnowing-basket wreathed with a snake and takes him to Kybele at Mount Ida (see OH 46i). This myth—or a similar one—might be behind Strabo’s notice that Sabazios-Dionysos is “in some way the child of Mother” (10.3.15): the qualification “in some way” suggests something along the lines of a nurse or adopted mother. The only other certain instances of Hipta’s name come from four inscriptions found in an area not too distant from Mount Tmolos in Lydia; see Morand 2001, pp. 177–181. On three of these inscriptions Sabazios-Zeus is also mentioned (see OH 48i). This pairing is mirrored in the placement of this hymn after the one to Sabazios. Hipta is addressed as “Mother” in all four, which strongly suggests an identification with Kybele; compare the vase painting mentioned in OH 46i. Such an identification might be intended in our hymn, since she is called “chthonic mother” (line 4) and connected with Mount Ida in Phrygia and Mount Tmolos (see OH 27i). That Proclus distinguishes between Hipta and Mother does not entail their separation in our collection; he might have had a different version of the story in mind, or tried to rationally reconcile two slightly different ones. 50. To Lysios Lenaios50. 致酒神吕西奥斯·勒奈奥斯
This hymn is dedicated to Dionysos under two epithets. The first one, “Lysios,” means “he that frees, he that sets loose, the redeemer.” The notion of freedom from restraint, whether this restraint be physical, social, or spiritual, was an essential part of the religious conception of Dionysos. Insofar as he is a god of transitions, he “loosens” the moorings that tie an individual to any particular fixity; see OH 30i. Myth reflects this particular trait: Dionysos cannot be bound (e.g., Homeric Hymn to Dionysos 7.13–15), and he can free others from their bonds (e.g., Euripides Bacchae 443–450); see also OH 47.5+n. Lysios was a cult title of Dionysos (see Pausanias 2.2.6–7, 2.7.5–6, and 9.16.6), found also at OH 52.2. It is used as an epithet at OH 42.4 (“redeeming”) as well as in lines 2 and 8 of this hymn. In Orphic contexts, Dionysos is said to be able to release one from madness and other suffering (see OH 53i) and even free an initiate from the guilt inherited from his murder at the hands of the Titans (Bacchic gold tablets no. 26a and b; see also Graf/Johnston 2007, pp. 132 and 147). Dionysos, more so than any of the other divinities in the collection, is the god that saves. Our poet, however, has evidently opted for a more limited view of Lysios, the one joined with the idea of the freedom of restraint as induced by intoxication. The second epithet, Lenaios, makes this clear, as it functions to limit the preceding Lysios. The word means “of the wine-press” (Greek “lēnos”; see Diodorus Siculus 3.63.4). It was a cult title of Dionysos at Athens and connected with the Lenaia festival, which was a celebration that took place every January. The Lenaia became an official venue for the performance of comedy and then eventually tragedy in the second half of the fifth century, although it was not as prestigious as the Greater Dionysia. We know very little about this festival. Of particular relevance is that officials from the Eleusinian Mysteries were involved in the procession and that part of the ritual involved the worshippers calling on the god as “son of Semele, Iacchos, giver of wealth” (for Iacchos, see OH 42.4n). While the name itself would seem to suggest this festival revolved around wine, modern scholars have favored a different interpretation that sees the name Lenaia as being derived from “lēnai,” another word for maenads (see OH 52i). And this etymology might very well have been on the mind of our initiates, for the name of the festival occurs at OH 54.9 in a clearly maenadic context (cf. line 8 of this hymn, which contains maenadic imagery). For more on the Lenaia, see Pickard-Cambridge 1988, pp. 25–42, and Larson 2007, pp. 134–135. Our hymn, however, focuses on Dionysos as the god of wine and its effects: the release from cares, the happiness it brings, and the ever-present danger of disorderly conduct. This ambiguity of the power of wine is seen in the story of Ikarios. When Dionysos comes to Attika, he is received hospitably by this man. In gratitude, Dionysos teaches him the secrets of making wine. Ikarios shares the fruits of his labor with some shepherds one night, who, later believing to have been poisoned, kill him (see Apollodoros 3.14.7). Normally, though, wine was seen as a beneficial gift the god gives to human beings as a temporary respite from their daily existence (e.g., Hesiod Works and Days 614 and Euripides Bacchae 280–282; see also OH 30i). Dionysos is often depicted in the iconography himself in the act of drinking or carrying the necessary accoutrements, usually accompanied by satyrs and/or maenads (e.g., Boardman 1975, pll. 6, 110, 256, and 343). He is intimately connected with the symposium and revelry. Wine can be thought of as the god himself (see Euripides Bacchae 284–285), who, when ingested, possesses the worshipper (enthousiasmos) and effects a state of ekstasis (see OH 30i).这首颂歌献给狄俄尼索斯，带有两个称号。第一个称号“吕西奥斯”意为“解放者、释放者、救赎者”。摆脱束缚——无论是身体、社会还是精神上的束缚——是狄俄尼索斯宗教观念的核心部分。作为过渡之神，他“解开”将个体束缚于任何特定固定状态的锚链；参见《俄耳甫斯颂歌》30i。神话反映了这一特质：狄俄尼索斯无法被束缚（如《荷马颂歌·致狄俄尼索斯》7.13–15），且能解放他人于枷锁之中（如欧里庇得斯《酒神的伴侣》443–450）；另见《俄耳甫斯颂歌》47.5+n。吕西奥斯是狄俄尼索斯的祭祀称号（见保萨尼阿斯《希腊志》2.2.6–7、2.7.5–6 及 9.16.6），亦出现于《俄耳甫斯颂歌》52.2。该称号在本颂歌第 2 行与第 8 行作为修饰语使用，亦见于《俄耳甫斯颂歌》42.4（“救赎的”）。在俄耳甫斯教语境中，狄俄尼索斯被认为能使人摆脱疯狂与其他苦难（见《俄耳甫斯颂歌》53i），甚至能解救信徒于因泰坦弑神而继承的罪孽（酒神金板第 26a 与 b 号；另见格拉夫/约翰斯顿 2007 年著作第 132 与 147 页）。在本颂歌集中，狄俄尼索斯较其他神祇更显著地扮演着救世主的角色。 然而，我们的诗人显然选择了对吕西奥斯更为局限的理解，即将其与醉酒所引发的无拘无束的自由感相联系。第二个称号"勒奈奥斯"明确了这一点，因为它起到了限制前一个称号"吕西奥斯"的作用。这个词意为"酒榨之神"（希腊语"lēnos"；参见狄奥多罗斯·西库卢斯《历史丛书》3.63.4）。这是狄俄尼索斯在雅典的一个崇拜称号，与每年一月举行的勒奈亚节有关。勒奈亚节在公元前五世纪下半叶成为喜剧乃至悲剧演出的官方场所，尽管其声望不及大狄俄尼索斯节。关于这个节日我们知之甚少。特别值得注意的是，厄琉息斯秘仪的官员参与了游行队伍，而仪式的一部分包括崇拜者呼唤这位神为"塞墨勒之子、伊阿科斯、财富的赐予者"（关于伊阿科斯，参见《俄耳甫斯颂歌》42.4 注释）。虽然节日名称本身似乎暗示其围绕葡萄酒展开，但现代学者倾向于另一种解释，认为"勒奈亚"一词源自"lēnai"——即酒神女祭司的别称（参见《俄耳甫斯颂歌》52i）。 这一词源很可能正是我们入会者心中所想，因为节日的名称出现在《俄耳甫斯颂歌》第 54.9 节中，其语境明显与酒神狂女相关（参见本颂歌第 8 行，其中包含酒神狂女的意象）。关于勒奈亚节的更多信息，请参阅皮卡德-坎布里奇 1988 年著作第 25-42 页，以及拉森 2007 年著作第 134-135 页。然而，我们的颂歌将狄俄尼索斯主要视为酒神及其效应之神：从忧虑中解脱、带来幸福，以及无序行为始终存在的危险。酒力量的这种双重性在伊卡里俄斯的故事中得以体现。当狄俄尼索斯来到阿提卡时，他受到了此人的热情款待。出于感激，狄俄尼索斯传授给他酿酒的秘密。一天晚上，伊卡里俄斯与一些牧羊人分享了他的劳动成果，后者后来误以为自己中毒，便杀死了他（参见阿波罗多洛斯《书库》3.14.7）。不过，通常酒被视为神赐予人类的恩惠，作为他们日常生活的暂时喘息（例如，赫西俄德《工作与时日》第 614 行和欧里庇得斯《酒神的伴侣》第 280-282 行；另见《俄耳甫斯颂歌》第 30i 节）。 在图像描绘中，狄俄尼索斯常被表现为正在饮酒或携带必要器具的形象，通常伴有萨提尔和/或迈那得斯（例如，Boardman 1975，图版 6、110、256 和 343）。他与酒宴和狂欢紧密相连。葡萄酒可以被视为神祇本身（参见欧里庇得斯《酒神的女祭司》第 284–285 行），当被饮下时，会占据崇拜者的身心（enthousiasmos），并引发一种出神状态（ekstasis）（参见《俄耳甫斯颂歌》30i）。
This hymn continues the theme of Dionysos’ birth (lines 1 and 3), and, as with previous hymns in this grouping (see OH 44i), contains a reference to a specific Dionysian cult. 51. To the Nymphs51. 致宁芙女神
The Greek word “numphē” generally refers to a young woman, either of marriageable age or newly-wed (see OH 71.1n), but it also signifies any of a variety of minor female deities of nature. Nymphs were connected with a number of geographical features: forests, trees, mountains, springs, and meadows (Odyssey 6.122–124, Homeric Hymn to Aphrodite 5.97–99). Groups often are called by specific names that reflect their topographical associations. Thus Dryads are nymphs of the trees (Greek “drus”), Oreads are nymphs of the mountains (Greek “oros”), Naiads are nymphs of the springs (from the Greek verb “naō,” “I flow”), and so forth; see also notes to lines 12 and 14. Nymphs are referred to as the daughters of Zeus by early poets (e.g., Iliad 6.420, Hesiod fragment 304, Alkaios fragment 343). The Ash Tree Nymphs, on the other hand, are born from the blood that drips from the severed genitals of Sky (Hesiod Theogony 183–187). Hesiod also gives the mountain nymphs a different genealogy, making them the sisters of the Kouretes and satyrs (see OH 31i and OH 54i). The Nereids and Okeanids (see line 1 and note), both pluralities of young women connected with natural features, could also be construed as nymphs. Our hymn identifies them specifically with the Okeanids at first but subtly widens the scope to include their traditional venues of woods, mountains, and meadows while stressing their connection with water (see note to lines 15–16). Rustic and pastoral settings away from civilization are their domain. Caves and grottos are favorite haunts. They are found running with Artemis, frolicking with Hermes and Pan (see note to line 8), or sporting with Eros, Aphrodite, and Dionysos (see OH 58.3n). They also are part of the Dionysian thiasos (see OH 54.6), and in some accounts they are the ones who raise the infant Dionysos after the death of Semele, as here (see line 3 and note). This last detail integrates the hymn in the series that focuses on Dionysos’ birth (see OH 44i). We capitalize “Nymphs” when they refer to this particular grouping.希腊语“numphē”一词通常指年轻女性，无论是适婚年龄还是新婚（参见 OH 71.1n 注释），但也泛指各类自然界的次要女神。宁芙与多种地理特征相关：森林、树木、山脉、泉水和草地（《奥德赛》6.122–124，《荷马颂歌·阿佛洛狄忒》5.97–99）。这些群体常以反映其地形关联的特定名称被称呼。例如，树宁芙（Dryads）是树木的宁芙（希腊语“drus”），山岳宁芙（Oreads）是山脉的宁芙（希腊语“oros”），水泽宁芙（Naiads）是泉水的宁芙（源自希腊动词“naō”，意为“我流动”），等等；另见第 12 行和第 14 行的注释。早期诗人将宁芙称为宙斯的女儿（例如，《伊利亚特》6.420，赫西俄德残篇 304，阿尔凯奥斯残篇 343）。另一方面，白蜡树宁芙则诞生自天空神被割下的生殖器滴落的血液（赫西俄德《神谱》183–187）。赫西俄德还为山岳宁芙提供了不同的谱系，使她们成为库瑞忒斯和萨提尔的姐妹（参见 OH 31i 和 OH 54i）。 涅瑞伊得斯与俄刻阿尼得斯（参见第 1 行及注释），这两类与自然景观相关的年轻女性群体，亦可被理解为宁芙。本颂诗最初明确将其与俄刻阿尼得斯等同，而后巧妙地将范围扩展至她们传统的活动场所——森林、山峦与草甸，同时强调她们与水的关联（参见第 15-16 行注释）。远离尘嚣的乡野与牧场景观是她们的领域，洞穴与岩窟是她们钟爱的栖居地。她们常与阿尔忒弥斯并肩奔跑，与赫尔墨斯及潘神嬉戏（参见第 8 行注释），或与厄洛斯、阿佛洛狄忒及狄俄尼索斯欢闹（参见《俄耳甫斯颂歌》58.3 注释）。她们亦是狄俄尼索斯狂欢队伍的一部分（参见《俄耳甫斯颂歌》54.6），在某些传说中——如本诗所述（参见第 3 行及注释）——她们正是在塞墨勒死后抚养幼年狄俄尼索斯的群体。这一最终细节使本颂诗融入了聚焦狄俄尼索斯诞生的系列篇章（参见《俄耳甫斯颂歌》44i）。当“宁芙”特指此类群体时，我们将其首字母大写。
Nymphs were widely worshipped in antiquity, almost always tied to a particular locale. Odysseus kisses the ground on his return to Ithaka and prays to the Naiads whose sacred cave is nearby (Odyssey 13.345–360). A famous cave to the nymphs and Pan on Mount Parnassos, the Korykian Cave, gained Panhellenic importance due to its proximity to Delphi. Any feature of the land could become a place to worship a nymph or group of nymphs. For more details on their cults, see Larson 2007, pp. 153–155. Nymphs were known to kidnap men that caught their fancy from time to time, such as Herakles’ friend Hylas (Apollonios of Rhodes Argonautika 1.1207–1239) and Hermaphroditos (Ovid Metamorphoses 4.285–388), a belief that survives in modern-day Greek folklore.在古代，宁芙女神受到广泛崇拜，几乎总是与特定的地点联系在一起。奥德修斯返回伊萨卡时亲吻大地，并向附近拥有神圣洞穴的那伊阿得斯祈祷（《奥德赛》13.345–360）。位于帕尔纳索斯山上著名的宁芙与潘神洞穴——科吕基安洞穴，因其靠近德尔斐而获得了泛希腊的重要性。陆地上的任何特征都可能成为崇拜一位或一群宁芙的场所。关于她们崇拜的更多细节，请参见拉森 2007 年，第 153–155 页。众所周知，宁芙会不时绑架引起她们兴趣的男子，例如赫拉克勒斯的朋友许拉斯（罗德岛的阿波罗尼奥斯《阿尔戈英雄纪》1.1207–1239）和赫马佛洛狄忒斯（奥维德《变形记》4.285–388），这一信仰在现代希腊民间传说中仍有留存。

52. To the God of Triennial Feasts52. 致三年节庆之神
This hymn is the first of a group of three that bring to a close the Dionysian, cultic section of the Hymns. The previous three hymns dedicated to Dionysos (OH 46, 47, 50) call on the god under specific cult titles. The titles of this hymn and the following two, in contrast, refer to general characteristics of cult rather than any specific one. “Triennial” refers to a celebration every two years (the ancient Greeks counted inclusively). While there were a number of festivals that occurred biennially (e.g., the Isthmian Games and Nemean Games), it appears that a large number of such celebrations were devoted to Dionysos, particularly maenadic ones, e.g., that of the Thyiads (Pausanias 10.4.3; see also Euripides Bacchae 133, Diodorus Siculus 4.3.2–3, Larson 2007, pp. 127–128, and further OH 46i). This hymn also follows the trend, as it primarily depicts the kind of processions that are typically performed by maenads (sometimes with satyrs; see OH 54i). While many of the traditional trappings of maenadic processions appear intermittently in the other Dionysian hymns of the collection, nearly all of them are mentioned here. The worshippers proceed at night, guided by torchlight (see OH 9.3n). They brandish thyrsi (see OH 45.5n) and wear fawn-skins. Madness seeps into them along with the god. Vigorous movement leading to wild dancing and singing creates a raucous revel (see note to lines 7–8). The ivy-wreathed group, the thiasos, heads to the mountains, where animals are ripped apart (sparagmos; see OH 11.9n, OH 30.5n, and OH 45.5n) and the raw flesh devoured (ōmophagia; see line 7 and note); other wondrous works, such as causing milk and wine to spring from the ground and the handling of snakes, are performed by the frenzied. To what extent this ideal reflects real practice and to what extent it is the result of the powerful images Euripides evokes in his Bacchae is something that is debated by scholars (see Larson 2007, pp. 136–137, with further references). Whatever the case may be, by the time our collection had been composed, such elements had become standard indications of ecstatic Dionysian worship and iconography, so much so that their appearance in the Hymns does not imply that the initiates were female, any more than the hymn to Eleusinian Demeter entails the group was located at Eleusis (and note that Kadmos and Teiresias dress up as maenads in Euripides Bacchae 169–214; cf. further Herodotos 4.79 and OH 54i). It is a routine rhetorical strategy in hymns to remind the gods of their favorite haunts and activities. This particular one focuses on Dionysos as the leader of processions. The god is often depicted in literature and art as participating in his own rituals among his worshippers (e.g., Euripides Bacchae 135–167; see also OH 53.6). In the Hymns, a number of female divinities are portrayed as maenads or described with maenadic imagery (see OH 1.3n), and Themis in her hymn founds maenadic rites (see OH 79.7–10+n). Such participation on the part of the gods helps blur the line between worshipped and worshipper, bringing the initiates into a more intimate contact with the powers they invoke (see OH 30i). There may have been a(nother) torch-lit procession at this point of the ritual (albeit probably not to a mountain), and Dionysos and his thiasos, upon finding such kindred spirits engaged in mimetic performances, would be more disposed to join the initiates in the ceremony. Triennial celebrations are mentioned at OH 30.5, OH 44.7, OH 53.4–5, and OH 54.3; see also Homeric Hymn to Dionysos 1.11.这首颂歌是三首一组中的第一首，标志着《颂歌集》中狄俄尼索斯崇拜部分的结束。之前三首献给狄俄尼索斯的颂歌（OH 46、47、50）以特定的崇拜称号呼唤这位神祇。相比之下，这首颂歌及随后两首的标题指的是崇拜的一般特征，而非任何特定的崇拜形式。"三年一度"指的是每两年举行一次的庆典（古希腊人采用包含计数法）。虽然有许多节日是每两年举行一次的（例如地峡运动会和尼米亚运动会），但似乎有大量此类庆典是献给狄俄尼索斯的，尤其是那些与酒神女信徒相关的庆典，例如提亚德斯女信徒的庆典（保萨尼阿斯《希腊志》10.4.3；另见欧里庇得斯《酒神的伴侣》第 133 行、狄奥多罗斯·西库卢斯《历史丛书》4.3.2–3、拉森 2007 年著作第 127–128 页，以及 OH 46i 的进一步说明）。这首颂歌也遵循了这一趋势，因为它主要描绘了通常由酒神女信徒（有时与萨提尔一起；参见 OH 54i）进行的游行类型。虽然酒神女信徒游行的许多传统元素在本集的其他狄俄尼索斯颂歌中零星出现，但几乎所有这些元素都在这里被提及。 信徒们在火炬的指引下于夜间行进（参见 OH 9.3 注释）。他们挥舞着酒神杖（参见 OH 45.5 注释），身披鹿皮。疯狂随着神祇一同渗入他们体内。剧烈的动作引发狂野的舞蹈与歌唱，形成喧闹的狂欢（参见第 7-8 行注释）。头戴常春藤花环的团体——酒神信徒队列——前往山中，在那里动物被撕裂（肢解仪式；参见 OH 11.9 注释、OH 30.5 注释及 OH 45.5 注释），生肉被吞食（生食仪式；参见第 7 行及注释）；其他奇迹般的举动，例如使奶与酒从地面涌出、徒手摆弄毒蛇，均由这些狂乱者完成。这种理想场景在多大程度上反映了真实实践，又在多大程度上是欧里庇得斯在《酒神的伴侣》中唤起的强烈意象所导致的结果，学者们对此存在争议（参见拉森 2007 年著作第 136-137 页，附更多参考文献）。 无论如何，到我们的诗集编纂完成时，这些元素已成为狂喜式狄俄尼索斯崇拜及其图像学的标准标志，以至于它们在《俄耳甫斯颂歌》中的出现，并不暗示入会者是女性，正如献给厄琉息斯的得墨忒耳的颂歌并不意味着该团体位于厄琉西斯（注意，在欧里庇得斯的《酒神的伴侣》第 169-214 行中，卡德摩斯和提瑞西阿斯装扮成迈那得斯；另见希罗多德《历史》4.79 及《俄耳甫斯颂歌》54i）。在颂歌中，提醒诸神他们钟爱的场所和活动是一种常规的修辞策略。这首特定的颂歌聚焦于狄俄尼索斯作为游行队伍的领导者。在文学和艺术中，这位神祇常被描绘为在信徒中参与自己的仪式（例如，欧里庇得斯《酒神的伴侣》第 135-167 行；另见《俄耳甫斯颂歌》53.6）。在《颂歌》中，多位女性神祇被描绘为迈那得斯或用迈那得斯的意象来描述（见《俄耳甫斯颂歌》1.3n），而忒弥斯在她的颂歌中创立了迈那得斯仪式（见《俄耳甫斯颂歌》79.7-10+n）。诸神的这种参与有助于模糊崇拜者与被崇拜者之间的界限，使入会者与他们所召唤的力量建立更亲密的联系（见《俄耳甫斯颂歌》30i）。 仪式进行到这一阶段时，或许曾有过（另一场）火炬游行（尽管很可能不是前往山岳），当狄俄尼索斯与其狂女团发现这些志趣相投的灵魂正进行着拟态表演时，会更倾向于加入入会者的仪式行列。《俄耳甫斯颂歌》第 30.5 首、第 44.7 首、第 53.4-5 首及第 54.3 首均提及三年一度的庆典；另可参见《荷马式狄俄尼索斯颂歌》1.11。

53. To the God of Annual Feasts53. 致年节之神
This is the last hymn to Dionysos in the collection, and it is closely related to the previous one (OH 52i). There, the emphasis is on maenadism. We find this theme here as well in lines 6–7, which serves as a bridge to the following hymn, but Dionysos is first and foremost presented as a god of vegetation, whose “awakening” in the spring heralds the return of plant-life after the winter; cf. the Thyiads at Delphi who wake Dionysos Liknites; see OH 46i. Plutarch reports a similar practice among the Phrygians and Paphlagonians, who believed a god was asleep in the winter, and he further says that the Phrygians awakened him in the summer by “Bacchizing” (De Iside et Osiride 378f). As our group of initiates might have been active in Phrygia, it is just possible that Plutarch is referring to the local rite that was made “Orphic” by the group (less likely the ritual itself). This is the only place in the collection where Dionysos is called “chthonic” (line 1), and his association with the underworld, where he “sleeps,” is indicated by the “sacred halls of Persephone” (line 3). The initiates invoke him with “fruity” terms (lines 8–10), and elsewhere in the collection he appears to be identified with the fruit itself (see OH 50.5+n). He is therefore much like Adonis and Persephone (see OH 56i and OH 41i, respectively), whose time split between the upper and lower worlds was interpreted as the cause of the seasons (and cf. line 7 of this hymn).
