54. To Silenos Satyros and the Bacchae54. 致西勒诺斯、萨提罗斯与酒神女信徒
This is the last hymn of the group whose overriding theme is Dionysian cult. It addresses the figure Silenos and mentions the other traditional members of the mythical Dionysian thiasos, the silens/satyrs and the Bacchae (or maenads); for the Bacchae, see OH 52i. The silens and satyrs were probably originally distinct, but very early merged into one group and their names are used interchangeably. The first mention of silens is on the François Vase (see Boardman 1991, pp. 33–34 and pl. 46), and satyrs are first mentioned by Hesiod (fragment 123, preserved at Strabo 10.3.19; see OH 51i). As line 7 of this hymn tells us, they are half-man, half-beast. Specifically, they are for the most part human, with equine tales and ears, snub noses, and a receding hairline; their bodies can be covered with hair, and early vase paintings sometimes give them hooves instead of feet. They are often shown ithyphallic. Sometimes they are found with hircine features. These are creatures of the wild, and they pursue quite a hedonistic lifestyle, spending their days laughing, drinking, dancing, making music, and chasing after nymphs (see, e.g., Homeric Hymn to Aphrodite 5.262–263). While originally independent of Dionysos, they became part of his retinue at an early date. They were insanely popular on vase paintings; see, for example, Hedreen’s 1992 book-length study (which only treats the Archaic period!). In myth, they play no significant role outside of being in the company of Dionysos (e.g., the story of the return of Hephaistos; see OH 66i). We find them as the chorus of a peculiar kind of drama, the satyr play, which was introduced with (or shortly after) Attic tragedy. In Classical times, a tragic poet would stage three tragedies followed by a satyr play at the Greater Dionysia. These performances were light-hearted affairs, aptly called “tragedy at play” by Demetrius (On Style 169). Despite the fact that the only extant satyr play is Euripides’ Kyklops, on the basis of this and numerous fragments we have some idea of the nature of this genre. Lissarrague neatly sums it up thus: “The recipe is as follows: take one myth, add the satyrs, and observe the results” (1990, p. 236). The chorus in a satyr play is led by Papposilenos (Granddaddy Silenos!), who is distinguished from the rest by being costumed as an old satyr, covered with white hair (as depicted on the Pronomos vase, which shows the actors at a rehearsal; see Boardman 1989, pp. 167–168 and pl. 323); he is the leader of the thiasos here as well (see line 6). Silenos occasionally plays a role in myth as a distinct individual. His most famous “exploit” is being found drunk in the garden of Midas, king of Phrygia. The king returns the lost satyr to Dionysos, who grants him a boon that turns into the famous “golden touch” (Ovid Metamorphoses 1.85–145). Another satyr, Marsyas, either invents the reed instrument known as the auloi or picks them up after Athene discards them (see OH 32i). He then challenges Apollon to a music contest in Phrygia, loses, and is flayed alive by the god (see Ovid Metamorphses 11.146–193). In cult, too, the satyrs are completely dependent on their master, although Pausanias does mention a temple for Silenos at Elis and stresses it is completely independent from Dionysos (6.24.8). Male worshippers of Dionysian ecstatic rituals could apparently take the role of satyrs, as well as pans, as is attested by Plato (Laws 815c–d) and by early rituals involving masks (see Burkert 1985, pp. 103–104); see also OH 52i. Satyrs and Silenos himself seem to be entirely ignored in Orphism, maybe because their light-hearted nature did not fit well with the serious cosmic and eschatological themes found in the mysteries (but see note to line 10 below). Their appearance in our collection is due to their traditional association with Dionysos. As they are followers of Dionysos, so, too, their hymn follows his. It is possible that our initiates dressed up as satyrs and Bacchae (perhaps just for this part of the ritual); see also OH 45i and OH 52i.这是该组颂歌中的最后一首，其核心主题是狄俄尼索斯崇拜。它提及了西勒诺斯这一形象，并提到了神话中狄俄尼索斯狂欢队伍的其他传统成员——西勒诺斯/萨提尔和巴克坎忒斯（或称迈那得斯）；关于巴克坎忒斯，参见《俄耳甫斯颂歌》第 52 首注释。西勒诺斯与萨提尔最初可能有所区别，但很早就融合为一个群体，它们的名称常被互换使用。西勒诺斯最早出现在弗朗索瓦陶瓶上（参见 Boardman 1991, pp. 33–34 及图版 46），而萨提尔则最早由赫西俄德提及（残篇 123，保存在斯特拉博《地理志》10.3.19 中；参见《俄耳甫斯颂歌》第 51 首注释）。如本颂歌第 7 行所述，它们是半人半兽的存在。具体而言，它们大部分具有人形，但长着马尾巴和马耳朵、塌鼻子和后退的发际线；身体可能覆盖毛发，早期陶瓶画有时将它们描绘成蹄足而非人脚。它们常被表现为勃起状态，偶尔带有山羊特征。这些是荒野的生灵，追求极度享乐的生活方式，终日欢笑、饮酒、舞蹈、奏乐并追逐宁芙（例如，参见《荷马颂歌·阿佛洛狄忒》5.262–263）。 虽然最初与狄俄尼索斯无关，但他们在早期便成为其随从的一部分。他们在花瓶绘画中极为流行；例如，可参见赫德林 1992 年的专著研究（仅涉及古风时期！）。在神话中，除了陪伴狄俄尼索斯外，他们并无重要角色（例如赫菲斯托斯归来的故事；参见《俄耳甫斯颂歌》66i）。我们发现他们是一种特殊戏剧——萨提尔剧的合唱队，这种戏剧与阿提卡悲剧同时（或稍后）出现。在古典时期，悲剧诗人会在大狄俄尼索斯节上演出三部悲剧，随后上演一部萨提尔剧。这些表演轻松愉快，被德米特里厄斯恰当地称为“嬉戏中的悲剧”（《论风格》169）。尽管唯一现存的萨提尔剧是欧里庇得斯的《独眼巨人》，但基于此剧及众多残篇，我们对这一体裁的性质有所了解。利萨拉格简洁地总结道：“配方如下：取一则神话，加入萨提尔，观察结果”（1990 年，第 236 页）。萨提尔剧中的合唱队由帕普西勒诺斯（西勒诺斯爷爷！）领导。), 他因装扮成老萨提尔而与众不同，全身覆盖着白色毛发（如普罗诺莫斯瓶画所示，描绘了排练中的演员；参见 Boardman 1989 年，第 167-168 页及图版 323）；他也是此处狂欢队伍的首领（见第 6 行）。西勒诺斯偶尔在神话中以独立个体的身份出现。他最著名的“壮举”是在弗里吉亚国王米达斯的花园中被发现醉酒。国王将迷途的萨提尔归还给狄俄尼索斯，后者赐予他一项恩惠，却演变为著名的“点石成金”能力（奥维德《变形记》1.85–145）。另一位萨提尔玛耳绪阿斯，要么发明了被称为奥洛斯管的芦苇乐器，要么在雅典娜丢弃后捡起了它们（参见《俄耳甫斯颂歌》32i）。随后他在弗里吉亚向阿波罗发起音乐挑战，失败后被神活活剥皮（参见奥维德《变形记》11.146–193）。在祭祀中，萨提尔们也完全依附于他们的主人，尽管保萨尼阿斯确实提到埃利斯有一座西勒诺斯的神庙，并强调它完全独立于狄俄尼索斯（6.24.8）。 狄俄尼索斯狂喜仪式的男性崇拜者显然可以扮演萨提尔和潘神的角色，这一点在柏拉图（《法律篇》815c–d）以及涉及面具的早期仪式中有所记载（参见 Burkert 1985, pp. 103–104）；另见 OH 52i。萨提尔和西勒诺斯本人在俄耳甫斯教中似乎被完全忽视，或许是因为他们轻松愉快的本性不太符合神秘仪式中严肃的宇宙论和末世论主题（但请参见下文第 10 行的注释）。他们在我们的文集中出现，是由于他们与狄俄尼索斯的传统联系。正如他们是狄俄尼索斯的追随者，他们的赞美诗也紧随其后。我们的新入教者可能装扮成萨提尔和巴克坎忒斯（也许仅用于仪式的这一部分）；另见 OH 45i 和 OH 52i。

55. To Aphrodite55. 致阿佛洛狄忒
Aphrodite is the goddess of love, beauty, and sexual relations. For Homer, she was the daughter of Zeus and Dione (Iliad 5.370–417), a goddess sometimes considered a Titan, sometimes a nymph (see OH O.19n); her name is a feminine variation of Zeus. Hesiod gives another account, in which she is born after Kronos castrates his father Sky and tosses the severed genitals into the sea. They undergo a sort of foamy chemical reaction out of which Aphrodite is born (Theogony 188–206). Hesiod’s story teems with etymological explanations. Aphrodite is so called because she was born from foam (Greek “aphros”). She bears the names Kythereia because she came to the island Kythera; and the name Kyprogenes because she first came out of the sea on Kypros and so was “born on Kypros.” She also took on the epithet “fond of genitals” because of their role in her birth. When she rises out of the sea, the Seasons are there to clothe her and deck her out with all sorts of finery, a scene memorably portrayed in Botticelli’s painting The Birth of Venus (compare also the sixth Homeric hymn). In Hesiod’s version, then, Aphrodite is thus a cosmic power that antedates Zeus and the other Olympian gods. Orphic mythology accepted the Hesiodic version, although in at least one variant it is Zelos (Envy) and Apate (Deception), not the Seasons, that welcome the goddess out of the sea (Orphic fragment 189; see also OH 3.2n). The Orphics, however, also maintained that she (or a second Aphrodite) was the daughter of Zeus but that Zeus created her by ejaculating into the sea (Orphic fragment 260).阿佛洛狄忒是爱情、美丽与性关系的女神。在荷马笔下，她是宙斯与狄俄涅之女（《伊利亚特》5.370–417），这位女神时而被视为泰坦神，时而被视为宁芙（参见 OH O.19n）；其名实为宙斯（Zeus）的阴性变体。赫西俄德则提供了另一种说法：克洛诺斯阉割其父乌拉诺斯后，将割下的生殖器抛入海中。这些器官在泡沫中发生某种化学反应，阿佛洛狄忒便由此诞生（《神谱》188–206）。赫西俄德的叙述充满词源学解释：因其诞生于泡沫（希腊语“aphros”）而得名阿佛洛狄忒；因曾抵达基西拉岛而获名库忒瑞亚；因最初从塞浦路斯海域现身而被称为“塞浦路斯诞生的”。由于生殖器在其诞生中的关键作用，她还获得了“喜爱生殖器”的别称。当她从海中升起时，时序女神为其披上衣袍并饰以华美珠宝——这一场景在波提切利画作《维纳斯的诞生》中得到传神描绘（亦可对照《荷马颂诗》第六首）。由此可见，在赫西俄德的版本中，阿佛洛狄忒实为早于宙斯及其他奥林匹斯诸神的宇宙级力量。 俄耳甫斯神话采纳了赫西俄德的版本，尽管至少有一种变体记载，迎接女神从海中诞生的并非时序女神，而是泽洛斯（嫉妒）与阿帕忒（欺骗）（俄耳甫斯残篇 189；另见 OH 3.2n）。然而，俄耳甫斯教派亦主张她（或第二位阿佛洛狄忒）是宙斯之女，但宙斯是通过将精液射入海中而创造了这位女神（俄耳甫斯残篇 260）。
Aphrodite was connected with both the carnal and spiritual sides of love, and accordingly literature portrays many sides of her. The Homeric Hymn to Aphrodite (no. 5) opens with a grand description of her powers: even Zeus is under her sway, and only three goddesses—Artemis, Athene, and Hestia—are immune to her charms (5.1–44). When Hera seeks to seduce Zeus to distraction during the Trojan War, she borrows a magical piece of clothing from Aphrodite, a concrete manifestation of the love goddess’ abilities (Iliad 14.197–223). Aphrodite is raised to a cosmic principle of procreation, much like in our hymn, in Lucretius’ opening address to her (On the Nature of Things 1.1–49), and she is endowed with further philosophical embellishment in the Neoplatonist Proclus’ second hymn. Yet there is a comical side to this goddess as well. She is caught having an affair with Ares by her husband, Hephaistos, and the entangled lovers are displayed to the male gods, whereupon Apollon and Hermes engage in some playful banter (Odyssey 8.266–366). It should be kept in mind that the bard in the story who sings this tale does so to cheer up the sorrowing Odysseus. Apollonios of Rhodes shows her as a frustrated mother at wit’s end on how to handle her unruly child Eros (Argonautika 3.1–166). There is a nasty side to this divinity, too. Helen meekly acquiesces to Aphrodite’s demand to go to bed with Paris after the goddess ominously warns her not to disobey (Iliad 3.383–420). She unceasingly victimizes the mortal Psyche, first by asking Eros to make her fall in love with a monster; then, after Eros saves Psyche only to be betrayed by her, Aphrodite imposes a series of impossibly difficult tasks that eventually lead to Eros rescuing Psyche and a reconciliation with Aphrodite (Apuleius Metamorphoses or The Golden Ass 4.28–6.24). There is also something sinister lurking in Sappho’s depiction of the goddess, who can cause someone to fall in love even if they are unwilling (fragment 1.21–24). Love can be pleasant, wonderful, charming, exhilarating, frightening, and brutal—often all at the same time—and the stories of Aphrodite provide firm evidence that the Greeks were acutely aware of this complexity.阿芙洛狄忒与爱的肉体和精神层面皆有联系，因此文学作品描绘了她的多面性。《荷马颂歌·致阿芙洛狄忒》（第五首）开篇以恢弘笔触描述她的力量：连宙斯亦受其支配，唯有三位女神——阿尔忒弥斯、雅典娜与赫斯提亚——能免疫她的魅力（5.1-44）。当赫拉在特洛伊战争期间企图引诱宙斯分神时，她向阿芙洛狄忒借来一件具有魔力的衣物，这成为爱神能力的具体体现（《伊利亚特》14.197-223）。如同本颂歌所述，卢克莱修在开篇致词中将阿芙洛狄忒提升为宇宙繁衍的法则（《物性论》1.1-49），而新柏拉图主义者普罗克洛斯的第二首颂歌更为她增添了哲学修饰。然而这位女神亦有滑稽的一面：她与阿瑞斯的私情被丈夫赫菲斯托斯撞破，纠缠的情侣被展示在众男神面前，引得阿波罗与赫尔墨斯戏谑调侃（《奥德赛》8.266-366）。需知故事中吟唱此诗的游吟诗人，正是为了抚慰忧伤的奥德修斯。 罗得岛的阿波罗尼奥斯将她描绘成一位束手无策的母亲，不知如何管教她那不守规矩的孩子厄洛斯（《阿尔戈英雄纪》3.1–166）。这位女神也有其险恶的一面。当阿芙洛狄忒不祥地警告海伦不得违抗时，海伦顺从地答应了女神的要求，与帕里斯同床共枕（《伊利亚特》3.383–420）。她不断折磨凡人普赛克，先是让厄洛斯使普赛克爱上怪物；随后，在厄洛斯救下普赛克却遭其背叛后，阿芙洛狄忒又强加一系列几乎不可能完成的任务，最终导致厄洛斯再次拯救普赛克，并与阿芙洛狄忒和解（阿普列乌斯《变形记》或《金驴记》4.28–6.24）。萨福对这位女神的描绘中也潜藏着某种不祥的气息，她能让不情愿的人也坠入爱河（残篇 1.21–24）。爱情可以是愉悦的、美妙的、迷人的、令人振奋的、可怕的、残酷的——常常同时具备所有这些特质——而阿芙洛狄忒的故事有力地证明，希腊人敏锐地意识到了这种复杂性。
At Symposium 180d–181c, Plato sharply distinguishes two cult manifestations of the goddess, Aphrodite Ourania (Aphrodite the Heavenly or Born from Sky) and Aphrodite Pandemos (Aphrodite of All the People). The former, for him, represents the spiritual side of love, while the latter the physical. However, in actual cult practice this distinction is not observed. Indeed, Aphrodite Pandemos is found worshipped as a deity promoting civic harmony, the power of love to soothe civil discord and bring opposing sides together (see note to line 9). Her daughter, Harmonia, may be seen as a reflection of this (see OH 65i). Not surprisingly, Aphrodite is also worshipped in connection with marriage, particularly the producing of children. She also protects sailors. For more on Aphrodite and her role in cult, see Burkert 1985, pp. 152–156, and Larson 2007, pp. 114–125. She is found connected with other male gods in both myth and cult, in particular Hermes, Ares, and Hephaistos; see OH 57.3–5n, OH 65i, OH 66i, respectively. The significance of these pairings seems largely to consist of a harmonious unison of opposites (male/female, life/death, war/peace, beauty/ugliness). We also find her connected with Dionysos in cult (Pausanias 7.25.9) and in our hymn (lines 2 and 7; compare “maddening” in line 13, and also see OH 56i). As a goddess of beauty, she often consorts with other beautiful goddesses, such as the Seasons and Graces (see OH 43i and OH 60i, respectively).在《会饮篇》180d–181c 中，柏拉图明确区分了女神的两种崇拜形态：阿芙洛狄忒·乌拉尼亚（天上的阿芙洛狄忒或生于天空者）与阿芙洛狄忒·潘德摩斯（全民的阿芙洛狄忒）。对他而言，前者代表爱的精神层面，而后者则代表肉体层面。然而，在实际的崇拜实践中，这种区分并未被严格遵守。事实上，阿芙洛狄忒·潘德摩斯被视为促进公民和谐的神祇，其爱的力量能够平息内部分歧并团结对立双方（参见第 9 行注释）。她的女儿哈耳摩尼亚可被视为这一特性的体现（参见《俄耳甫斯颂歌》65i）。毫不意外，阿芙洛狄忒也与婚姻崇拜相关，尤其是与生育子女有关。她还保护水手。关于阿芙洛狄忒及其在崇拜中的角色，更多内容可参见伯克特 1985 年著作第 152–156 页，以及拉尔森 2007 年著作第 114–125 页。在神话与崇拜中，她常与其他男性神祇产生关联，特别是赫尔墨斯、阿瑞斯和赫菲斯托斯；分别参见《俄耳甫斯颂歌》57.3–5 注释、《俄耳甫斯颂歌》65i 及《俄耳甫斯颂歌》66i。这些配对的意义似乎主要在于对立面的和谐统一（男/女、生/死、战争/和平、美/丑）。 我们还在祭祀（保萨尼阿斯 7.25.9）和本颂诗（第 2 行和第 7 行；比较第 13 行的“令人疯狂”，另见 OH 56i）中发现她与狄俄尼索斯相关联。作为美丽女神，她常与其他美丽女神相伴，例如时序女神和惠美女神（分别参见 OH 43i 和 OH 60i）。
The placement of this hymn resumes the series of major Olympian gods that had been interrupted by a long digression on divinities associated with Dionysos, and the resumption is facilitated by Aphrodite’s connection to him (see further OH 69i). The hymns to Adonis (OH 56), Eros (OH 58), and the Graces (OH 60) are grouped with her for obvious reasons. Chthonic Hermes (OH 57) is said to be her son in his hymn, while the Fates (OH 59) also appear to have been conceived as connected with Aphrodite, perhaps as her daughters (see note to line 3 and OH 59i), thus forming a triplet with Chthonic Hermes and Eros. OH 61–68 may also be considered part of the “Aphrodite” group; see OH 61i, OH 65i, and OH 68i.本颂诗的编排恢复了主要奥林匹亚神祇的序列，这一序列曾被一段关于狄俄尼索斯相关神祇的长篇离题所打断，而阿佛洛狄忒与他的联系促进了序列的恢复（详见 OH 69i）。阿多尼斯颂诗（OH 56）、厄洛斯颂诗（OH 58）和惠美女神颂诗（OH 60）因明显原因与她归为一组。冥界赫尔墨斯（OH 57）在其颂诗中被描述为她的儿子，而命运女神（OH 59）似乎也被构想为与阿佛洛狄忒相连，或许是她的女儿（参见第 3 行注释及 OH 59i），从而与冥界赫尔墨斯和厄洛斯形成三重组合。OH 61–68 也可被视为“阿佛洛狄忒”组的一部分；参见 OH 61i、OH 65i 和 OH 68i。
1 heavenly, smiling Aphrodite, praised in many hymns: The first word of the hymn, “heavenly,” is one of the main cult titles of the goddess (Aphrodite Ourania). “Smiling” is a translation of the Greek “philommeidēs,” which literally means “fond of smiles.” The word, like the similar “philommēdēs” (“fond of genitals”), is a common epithet of the goddess, who is often portrayed as smiling. Aphrodite is indeed “praised in many hymns”: there are three Homeric hymns dedicated to her (nos. 5, 6, 10), two hymns by Proclus (nos. 2, 5), and literary pieces in the hymnic style, including Sappho fragments 1 and 2 and the opening of Lucretius’ On the Nature of Things. The reference to “many hymns” probably is first and foremost to the ubiquity of her worship through the identification with similar goddesses in other traditions and thus anticipates lines 17–19. This hymn, then, is imagined as following worthy precedents.1 天上，微笑的阿芙洛狄忒，在众多颂歌中受赞颂：颂歌的首词“天上”是这位女神（阿芙洛狄忒·乌拉尼亚）的主要崇拜称号之一。“微笑”是对希腊语“philommeidēs”的翻译，字面意思是“喜爱微笑”。这个词与类似的“philommēdēs”（“喜爱生殖器”）一样，是这位女神的常见修饰语，她常被描绘为面带微笑。阿芙洛狄忒确实“在众多颂歌中受赞颂”：有三首荷马颂歌献给她（第 5、6、10 首），普罗克洛斯的两首颂歌（第 2、5 首），以及颂歌风格的文学作品，包括萨福的片段 1 和 2 以及卢克莱修《物性论》的开篇。提及“众多颂歌”很可能首先是指通过与其他传统中类似女神的认同，她的崇拜无处不在，从而预示了第 17 至 19 行。因此，这首颂歌被想象为遵循了值得称道的先例。
3 mother of Necessity: Necessity (Greek Anankē) is a divinity who plays a role in Orphic theogony. She mates with Time in the form of a winged serpent, and their children are Ether and Khaos (Orphic fragment 77, 110–113; see West 1983, pp. 70, 194–197, and 231 for more details). If “necessity” in the hymn to the Fates should be personified, then our poet would appear to have conceived them to be the daughters of Aphrodite (see OH 59.18n). Necessity is identified with Adrasteia in Orphism. As Adrasteia can sometimes be identified with Nemesis, the inevitability of Nemesis might also explain the position of OH 61–64 in the collection (see OH 61i). The idea of compulsion appears in the imagery of yoking (lines 4, 13, 14); compare also Homeric Hymn to Aphrodite 5.33–43, Sappho fragment 1.21–24, and PGM 4.2934.3 必然之母：必然（希腊语 Anankē）是俄耳甫斯神谱中的一位神祇。她以带翼巨蛇的形态与时间结合，诞下以太与卡俄斯（俄耳甫斯残篇 77, 110–113；详见 West 1983 年著作第 70、194–197 及 231 页）。若《命运女神颂》中的“必然”需拟人化，则本诗作者似乎将其构想为阿佛洛狄忒之女（参见 OH 59.18 注释）。在俄耳甫斯教义中，必然与阿德剌斯忒亚被视为同一存在。因阿德剌斯忒亚常与涅墨西斯混同，涅墨西斯的不可抗拒性亦可解释 OH 61–64 在诗集序列中的位置（参见 OH 61 导言）。强制的意象体现于轭具隐喻中（第 4、13、14 行）；另可对照《荷马颂诗·致阿佛洛狄忒》5.33–43、萨福残篇 1.21–24 及《希腊魔法纸莎草》4.2934。
4–7: Aphrodite’s wide-ranging powers are expressed through their geographical extent over the sky, earth, and sea, a rhetorical strategy employed in describing the powers of other gods as well; of particular relevance here are the hymns to Rhea (OH 14.9–10) and the Mother of the Gods (OH 27.4–8); see further OH 10.14–16n. Eros is similarly described in his hymn, although his powers extend beneath the earth as well (OH 58.5–7). See also Homeric Hymn to Aphrodite 5.2–6, Euripides Hippolytos 447–451, and Lucretius On the Nature of Things 1.1–27.4-7：阿佛洛狄忒的广泛神力通过其在天、地、海三界的疆域得以展现，这种修辞手法亦用于描述其他神祇的权能；与此尤为相关的是对瑞亚（《俄耳甫斯颂歌》14.9-10）与诸神之母（《俄耳甫斯颂歌》27.4-8）的颂诗；详见《俄耳甫斯颂歌》10.14-16 注。厄洛斯在其颂歌中亦被类似描述，然其权能更延伸至地底（《俄耳甫斯颂歌》58.5-7）。另可参阅《荷马颂诗·阿佛洛狄忒》5.2-6、欧里庇得斯《希波吕托斯》447-451 及卢克莱修《物性论》1.1-27。
8 Erotes: A divinity may sometimes be conceived as a plurality, as for example Pan and Eileithyia (see OH 2i and Burkert 1985, pp. 170–171). Pindar also makes Aphrodite the mother of Erotes (fragment 122.4), and Proclus gives the group a Neoplatonic interpretation in his second hymn at line 3 (see van den Berg 2001, pp. 199–200).8 厄洛特斯群神：神性有时可被构想为复数形态，如潘神与厄勒提亚（参见《俄耳甫斯颂歌》2i 及伯克特 1985 年著作第 170-171 页）。品达亦将阿佛洛狄忒奉为厄洛特斯之母（残篇 122.4），普罗克洛斯在其第二首颂诗第 3 行中赋予该神群新柏拉图主义阐释（参见范登伯格 2001 年著作第 199-200 页）。
9 Persuasion: Sometimes Persuasion is conceived as a separate goddess. She was worshipped together with Aphrodite at Athens (Pausanias 1.22.3). Sappho makes her the daughter of Aphrodite (fragment 200). In the decking out of Pandora, Persuasion joins the Graces in placing necklaces around her neck, while the Seasons crown her with a garland of spring flowers (Hesiod Works and Days 73–75). She is thus conceived as part of the traditional retinue of Aphrodite. One of the Okeanids is named Persuasion (Hesiod Theogony 349), and this might be the same Persuasion in the Pandora episode. In Orphic theogony, Eros and Persuasion are the parents of Hygeia (see OH 68i). Aphrodite’s connection with persuasion is a function both of its utility in amatory pursuits as well as its benefits in forging a consensus in public affairs.9 说服：有时说服被构想为独立的女神。她在雅典与阿芙洛狄忒一同受崇拜（保萨尼阿斯 1.22.3）。萨福将她视为阿芙洛狄忒的女儿（残篇 200）。在装扮潘多拉时，说服与美惠女神一同为她戴上项链，而时序女神则以春花编织的花冠为她加冕（赫西俄德《工作与时日》73–75）。因此她被构想为阿芙洛狄忒传统随从的一部分。其中一位俄刻阿尼得斯被命名为说服（赫西俄德《神谱》349），这可能与潘多拉故事中的说服是同一存在。在俄耳甫斯神谱中，厄洛斯与说服是许癸厄亚的父母（参见《俄耳甫斯颂歌》68i）。阿芙洛狄忒与说服的关联，既体现了说服在爱情追求中的实用性，也展现了它在公共事务中达成共识的益处。
15–28: The second half of this poem, equal in length to the first half, is an extended invocation to the goddess to appear, and it includes a list of places where the goddess might be. It is typical of the hymnic style to attract the attention of the addressee by calling to mind their favored locales, which often have specific cultic importance. This is the significance of the mention of Kypros, one of her most important cult sites and traditionally the place where she first stepped onto land after she was born. The other locations broaden her associations. Olympos is mentioned first, as she is naturally conceived above all as a Greek goddess. This also places her in the sky, and the further mention of land and sea recalls the three realms over which Aphrodite was earlier said to have dominion (lines 4–7). Syria points to her connection with the Semitic goddess Astarte, already identified with Aphrodite by Herodotos (1.150), while Egypt alludes to Isis. Aphrodite is included in a long list of deities identified with Moon/Isis in Apuleius Metamorphoses or The Golden Ass 11.2 and 11.5, as well as an even longer list in the first hymn to Isis by Isidoros (line 24, and note that the Syrian Astarte appears in line 18). 15–28：本诗后半部分与前半部分篇幅相当，是对女神降临的延展性祈求，其中列举了女神可能现身的地点。通过唤起受祈者对所钟爱之地的记忆来吸引其注意，是颂诗风格的典型特征，这些地点通常具有特定的宗教意义。提及塞浦路斯正体现了这一点——这是她最重要的祭祀圣地之一，传统上也被认为是她诞生后首次踏足陆地之处。其他地点则拓展了她的关联性。奥林匹斯山被首先提及，因为她首先被理解为希腊女神。这也将她置于天际，随后对陆地与海洋的提及则呼应了前文所述阿芙洛狄忒统辖的三重领域（第 4–7 行）。叙利亚指向她与闪米特女神阿斯塔特的关联（希罗多德已在《历史》1.150 中将阿斯塔特与阿芙洛狄忒等同），埃及则暗指伊西斯。在阿普列乌斯《变形记》（或称《金驴记》）11.2 与 11.5 中，阿芙洛狄忒被列入与月神/伊西斯等同的众神名录。5，以及在伊西多尔献给伊西斯的第一首赞美诗中更长的列表（第 24 行，注意叙利亚的阿斯塔特出现在第 18 行）。

56. To Adonis56. 致阿多尼斯
Adonis is an old Near Eastern divinity of vegetation and fertility. His name is derived from the Semitic “adon” (“lord”), and he is a counterpart to the Babylonian Tammuz, who is loved by a fertility goddess (Ishtar), dies an untimely death, and is ritually lamented. Another similar figure is Attis, who is a lover of the great mother goddess Kybele; see OH 27i. The worship of Adonis seems to have come first to Kypros and from there to have spread to Greece. Therefore, not only his nature but also his earlier sojourn to Kypros explains his special connection with Aphrodite (see OH 55i; for her similarity with Ishtar, see Burkert 1985, p. 155). However, it appears that the Greeks, as they often did with foreign imports, adapted Adonis and his worship to their own mythological and religious framework. His Eastern connection is made clear by the various genealogies given by Apollodoros (3.13.3–4): his father is either Phoinix, Kinyras (a refugee from the East who became king of Kypros), or Theias, king of Assyria. He is the product of an incestuous union between a father and his daughter, named Myrrh or Smyrna, who is transformed into a myrrh tree out of which Adonis is born (see also Antoninus Liberalis 34 and Ovid Metamorphoses 10.298–518; note that the story in Ovid is narrated by Orpheus). Endowed with exquisite beauty, he catches the eye of Aphrodite herself and becomes her paramour. In one account, Aphrodite is already in love with Adonis as an infant. She places him in a chest and hands him over to Persephone for safekeeping. Persephone also becomes enamored of the child and later refuses to give him back to Aphrodite. They appeal to Zeus for a resolution. He decrees that Adonis must spend one third of the year with Persephone, another third with Aphrodite, and the remaining third with the goddess of his choice; he opts to spend this third with Aphrodite. Thus Adonis, like Persephone, spends part of his time in the land of death and the other part in the land of living, and, insofar as he is a god of vegetation, this tale corroborates the dying of plant life in the sweltering heat of the summer (see also OH 53i). The story is also reminiscent of the dispute between Hermes and Apollon in the longer Homeric Hymn to Hermes (no. 4): the younger half-sibling appropriating the property of the older one, their squabble, and the appeal to their father, Zeus. As a young man, Adonis becomes quite fond of hunting, which eventually leads to his death at the tusks of a wild boar. Adonis was worshipped by women throughout the Greek world, who would ritually lament his death every year. Our earliest reference to the practice comes from Sappho (fragment 140), but we know about it chiefly as it was practiced at Athens in the Classical period. In the summer, seeds were sown in broken pots and taken to the roofs of homes after the plants sprouted. There these “Gardens of Adonis” were left to wither and die. The women loudly and expressively mourned the death of the god. They then laid out figures representing Adonis in a symbolic burial and afterward disposed of the “body” and the pots into the sea. For references and details of this practice, see Burkert 1985, pp. 176–177, and Larson 2007, p. 124. Theokritos devotes an entire idyll to an elaborate festival at Alexandria (Idyll 15), and Lucian mentions the worship of Adonis at Byblos, where the women at first mourn the dead Adonis and then celebrate his rebirth (On the Syrian Goddess 6–7). 57. To Chthonic Hermes57. 致冥界赫尔墨斯
The first hymn to Hermes already hinted at the god’s connection with the dead (OH 28.2), but this function has apparently taken a life of its own and achieved the status of a (quasi-)separate divinity in this hymn. Much like Hades can be called Chthonic Zeus, so here Chthonic Hermes is distinguished from Hermes, even though the two divinities are not kept entirely independent of one another (cf. also OH 73i). The role of Hermes as psukhopompos (guide of the souls) is well attested in the earliest Greek literature and is punned in the Greek on line 6 (“psukhais pompos,” translated as “the souls you bring”). In the Odyssey, the god shepherds the souls of the dead suitors to the underworld (24.1–14), and in the Homeric Hymn to Hermes, guiding the dead is listed among the god’s various functions (4.572). Hermes can also, when occasion calls for it, lead out from the land of the dead, as he does Persephone in the Homeric Hymn to Demeter (2.375–386). Hermes was also psukhopompos in Orphism (Orphic fragment 339), but it is curious that he is hardly mentioned in the extant sources and does not appear at all on the Bacchic gold tablets. The silence might very well be because his role is simply assumed. Perhaps, though, at least in some cases such as the gold tablets, the middleman might have been purposely left out in favor of the initiate’s soul proactively (with the help of the instructions) taking matters into its own hands (thus further differentiating the initiate from the uninitiated). Outside of Orphic cult, we find Hermes worshiped as Chthonic Hermes in connection with pouring libations to the dead; for details, see Burkert 1985, pp. 157–158, and Larson 2007, pp. 149–150. It is also curious to find Dionysos in particular as the father of Chthonic Hermes, since in literature and art Hermes is at times depicted as bringing the newly-born infant Dionysos to the nymphs of Nysa and/or Silenos (e.g., Apollodoros 3.4.3, Boardman 1989, pl. 126). Hermes and Aphrodite are often linked in cult (see Burkert 1985, pp. 220–221), but not as mother and son. The source and significance of this parentage of Chthonic Hermes remains a puzzle. In any event, this makes Persephone, who gives him his “high office” (line 9–10), his grandmother.3-5：此处给出的谱系在文献中独一无二，与《俄耳甫斯颂歌》28.1（宙斯与迈亚）所表达的传统谱系截然不同。尤其令人好奇的是，狄俄尼索斯竟被指定为冥界赫尔墨斯之父——因为在文学与艺术作品中，赫尔墨斯常被描绘为将初生的婴儿狄俄尼索斯送往尼萨山宁芙和/或西勒诺斯处的形象（例如阿波罗多洛斯《书库》3.4.3，博德曼 1989 年图版 126）。赫尔墨斯与阿芙洛狄忒在祭祀中常有关联（参见伯克特 1985 年著作第 220-221 页），但从未以母子关系出现。冥界赫尔墨斯这一身世来源及其意义至今仍是未解之谜。无论如何，这使得授予他"崇高权位"（第 9-10 行）的珀耳塞福涅成为了他的祖母。
4 Paphian maiden: Paphos, a city on the island of Kypros, had one of the oldest and most famous cult centers of Aphrodite.4 帕福斯少女：帕福斯是塞浦路斯岛上的城市，拥有最古老、最著名的阿芙洛狄忒祭祀中心之一。
6 destined harbor: Maybe a reference to Kharon, the one who conveys the dead across a river to the underworld proper, if not a general metaphor for the land of the dead.6 命定之港：若非泛指死者之地的隐喻，或指摆渡亡魂跨越冥河前往地府本境的卡戎。
7–8: The wand of Hermes is one of his most prominent attributes. Its ability to lull to sleep and to awaken are already mentioned in Homer; in particular note Odyssey 24.2–5, where, after describing the powers of this wand, the poet shows Hermes leading the souls of the dead with it. In our text the powers of sleep merge with the powers of death; for the close connection of the two concepts in Greek thought, see OH 85i. It is not clear what is intended in these lines. It may refer to the Orphic belief that souls are reborn. Another possibility is that they refer to the initiate’s expectations in the afterlife—that it is in fact the prerogative of Chthonic Hermes, as the agent of Persephone, to “awaken” those souls who have been put to “sleep” so that they may find their way to their special place in the underworld, as the Bacchic gold tablets describe.7-8：赫尔墨斯的权杖是他最显著的标志之一。其催眠与唤醒的能力在荷马史诗中已有提及；尤其值得注意的是《奥德赛》24.2-5，诗人在描述这根权杖的力量后，展现了赫尔墨斯用它引领死者灵魂的场景。在我们的文本中，睡眠之力与死亡之力相互交融；关于这两个概念在希腊思想中的紧密联系，参见 OH 85i。这几行诗的意图并不明确。可能指的是俄耳甫斯教关于灵魂重生的信仰。另一种可能是，它们指的是信徒对来世的期望——事实上，作为珀耳塞福涅的使者，冥界赫尔墨斯拥有“唤醒”那些被“催眠”的灵魂的特权，使它们能够找到通往冥界特定归宿的道路，正如酒神金版所描述的那样。
58. To Eros58. 致厄洛斯
Eros, better known under his Latin name Cupid, has become a familiar figure in the Western literary and iconographical tradition. He is the playful winged and cherubic child, flitting around with his little bow and arrows, capriciously shooting the unwitting and causing them to fall desperately in love—ofttimes, alas, with tragic effect. The fanciful juxtaposition of great power with the even greater irresponsibility of a child betrays a profound psychological insight in the experience of love that first takes root in the earliest of the lyric poets; see the references in the note to line 3. Our hymn elects not to ignore this poetic conceit but having paid sufficient homage to it, quickly passes over to the other side of Eros, the cosmic force of love and attraction that is essential to the chain of copulations that underlies the anthropomorphizing tales of creation. This Eros is among the oldest divinities in Hesiod, coming after Khaos and coeval with Earth and Tartaros (Theogony 116–122), and Sappho offers a similarly ancient pedigree by making him the son of Earth and Sky (fragment 198). In Orphism, Eros is identified with Protogonos, another primeval figure; see OH 6i+5–7n, and compare the mock theogony in Aristophanes’ Birds, where Eros’ role is analogous to that of Protogonos in Orphism (see OH 6.2n). It is perhaps a different Eros that becomes the companion to Aphrodite after her birth (Orphic fragment 261; compare Hesiod Theogony 201–202), and the father of Hygeia (with Persuasion her mother; see Orphic fragment 262 and further OH 68i). However, in more conventional genealogies he is the son of Aphrodite, as he is in our collection (OH 55.8), while the father is variously said to be Zeus, Hermes, or Ares (if a father is even mentioned, which often is not the case). Another account, attributed to the semi-legendary Olen, claims that Eros was the son of Eileithyia, the goddess of childbirth (see OH 2i). This is mentioned by Pausanias in his brief description of the worship of Eros at Thespiai, and he notes a few other cult centers (9.27.1–4). There is perhaps an allusion to Orphic myth in Simias’ (early third century BC) pattern poem Wings, where the winged child Eros is bearded and explains this anomaly by referring to his great antiquity, claiming to have been born in the earliest times when Necessity was in charge and denying to be the child of Aphrodite and Ares. Ether and Khaos are also mentioned, although textual corruption makes it difficult to know in what capacity. The poem ends with Eros describing his powers: he rules with gentleness (implicitly contrasting himself favorably to Necessity) and the earth, sea, and sky all yield to him. This assertion of wide-ranging power and the fusion of the cosmic with the literary are quite similar to what we find in this hymn.厄洛斯，更为人熟知的是其拉丁名丘比特，已成为西方文学与图像传统中一个耳熟能详的形象。他是那个顽皮、长着翅膀、如小天使般的孩子，手持小巧的弓箭四处飞舞，任性妄为地射向毫无防备的人们，使他们陷入绝望的恋爱——唉，常常带来悲剧性的后果。这种将巨大力量与孩童更甚的不负责任奇特地并置，揭示了爱情体验中深刻的心理学洞见，这一洞见最早植根于抒情诗人的初期创作；参见第 3 行注释中的相关引述。我们的颂歌并未忽视这一诗意的构想，但在充分致敬之后，迅速转向了厄洛斯的另一面——作为宇宙的爱与吸引力，这一力量对于一系列交配链至关重要，这些交配链构成了拟人化创世故事的基础。这个厄洛斯是赫西俄德笔下最古老的神祇之一，紧随卡俄斯之后，与盖亚和塔尔塔罗斯同时代（《神谱》116-122），而萨福则通过将他塑造为大地与天空之子（残篇 198），赋予了他同样古老的谱系。 在俄耳甫斯教中，厄洛斯被等同于普罗托戈诺斯，另一位原始神祇；参见《俄耳甫斯颂歌》6i+5–7n，并比较阿里斯托芬《鸟》中的戏仿神谱，其中厄洛斯的角色类似于俄耳甫斯教中的普罗托戈诺斯（见《俄耳甫斯颂歌》6.2n）。或许在阿佛洛狄忒诞生后成为其伴侣的是另一位厄洛斯（俄耳甫斯教残篇 261；比较赫西俄德《神谱》201–202），并且是许癸厄亚的父亲（其母为劝诱女神佩托；见俄耳甫斯教残篇 262 及《俄耳甫斯颂歌》68i）。然而，在更传统的谱系中，他是阿佛洛狄忒之子，正如我们这部文集所述（《俄耳甫斯颂歌》55.8），而其父亲则被不同地说是宙斯、赫尔墨斯或阿瑞斯（如果提及父亲的话，但通常并不提及）。另一种说法，归功于半传奇的奥伦，声称厄洛斯是分娩女神厄勒梯亚之子（见《俄耳甫斯颂歌》2i）。保萨尼阿斯在其对忒斯皮埃厄洛斯崇拜的简短描述中提到了这一点，并提到了其他几个崇拜中心（9.27.1–4）。 或许在公元前三世纪早期的西米亚斯的图案诗《翅膀》中，暗指了俄耳甫斯神话，诗中带翼的孩童厄洛斯长着胡须，他通过提及自己的古老起源来解释这一异常现象，声称自己诞生于最早的时代，那时由必然性主宰，并否认自己是阿芙洛狄忒和阿瑞斯的孩子。诗中还提到了以太和卡俄斯，尽管文本的损坏使我们难以了解它们的具体角色。诗歌以厄洛斯描述自己的力量结束：他以温柔统治（暗示自己比必然性更优越），大地、海洋和天空都屈服于他。这种对广泛权力的主张以及宇宙与文学的融合，与我们在本颂歌中所见极为相似。
2 who runs swiftly on a path of fire: The Greek word used here, “puridromos,” is also used of the Stars (OH 7.9), Sun (OH 8.11), and Astrapaios Zeus (OH 20.2). It gives Eros a celestial coloring, anticipating the transition from the chubby archer boy to sublime cosmic power.2 在火之路径上疾驰者：此处使用的希腊词“puridromos”也用于描述星辰（《俄耳甫斯颂歌》7.9）、太阳（《俄耳甫斯颂歌》8.11）和闪电之神宙斯（《俄耳甫斯颂歌》20.2）。这为厄洛斯赋予了天体的色彩，预示了他从圆胖的弓箭手孩童向崇高的宇宙力量的转变。
3 who plays together with gods and mortal men: The description of the power of love as “play” occurs in early Greek lyric; see for example Alkman PMGF 58 and Anakreon PMG 358. Anakreon PMG 357 is a mock prayer to Dionysos asking the god to be a “good counselor” to Kleoboulos (with a pun on this name, which means “famous for counsel”—and possibly also a play on Eubouleus, an alternate name of Dionysos; see OH 41.8n). In this poem, Dionysos is described as playing with Eros, nymphs, and Aphrodite. The poem was composed for a symposiastic setting, a situation where wine and love frequently mingled. The setting is the same for Plato’s aptly named Symposium, where the nature of Eros is discussed (see also Plato’s Phaedrus). A natural link between Eros and Dionysos is their ability to cause madness. Indeed, another fragment of Anakreon calls the dice of Eros “madness and battle” (PMG 398); the word “battle” is Homeric, and Anakreon is probably suggesting the Trojan War, whose immediate cause was passion. Apollonios of Rhodes portrays Eros cheating at dice against Ganymede (Argonautika 3.111–130).3 与神祇和凡人同乐者：将爱的力量描述为“游戏”见于早期希腊抒情诗；例如，可参考阿尔克曼《残篇集》第 58 首及阿那克里翁《残篇集》第 358 首。阿那克里翁《残篇集》第 357 首是一首对狄俄尼索斯的戏谑祷词，祈求这位神祇成为克勒奥布洛斯的“良谋者”（此处双关了其名“以谋略闻名”之意——可能也暗指狄俄尼索斯的别名欧布琉斯；参见《俄耳甫斯颂歌》41.8 注）。在这首诗中，狄俄尼索斯被描绘为与厄洛斯、宁芙和阿佛洛狄忒一同嬉戏。此诗创作于宴饮场合，这种情境中酒与爱常交融共生。柏拉图那部恰如其名的《会饮篇》亦设定于此种场景，其中探讨了厄洛斯的本质（另见柏拉图的《斐德若篇》）。厄洛斯与狄俄尼索斯之间的天然联系在于二者皆能引发迷狂。事实上，阿那克里翁的另一残篇称厄洛斯的骰子为“狂乱与争战”（《残篇集》第 398 首）；“争战”一词源自荷马史诗，阿那克里翁很可能暗指特洛伊战争——其直接起因正是情欲。罗德岛的阿波罗尼俄斯则描绘了厄洛斯在与伽倪墨得斯掷骰子时作弊的情景（《阿尔戈英雄纪》3.111–130）。
4 two-natured: Other divinities in the collection are two-natured (which probably refers to their androgyny), the most relevant being Protogonos (OH 6.1+n), who is equated with (the cosmic) Eros in Orphism (see the introduction to this hymn). Antagoras of Rhodes (see the note to lines 5–7 below) employs a synonymous epithet. For other androgynous divinities in the collection, see OH 9.4n.4 双重本性：本诗集中其他神祇亦具双重本性（可能指其雌雄同体特质），其中最相关的是原初之神（OH 6.1+n），在俄耳甫斯教派中与（宇宙）厄洛斯等同（参见本颂诗引言）。罗德岛的安塔戈拉斯（参见下文第 5-7 行注释）使用了同义修饰语。关于本诗集中其他雌雄同体的神祇，参见 OH 9.4n。
5–7: Compare the geographical extent with Aphrodite’s at OH 55.4–7; for this theme elsewhere in the collection, see OH 10.14–16n. The reference to the underworld (“of all that lies in Tartaros”) perhaps is intended to recall Orpheus’ charming of Hades and Persephone when he descended to their realm in order to bring back his beloved Eurydike; see OH 87.9n and cf. Ovid Metamorphoses 5.359–384 and 10.25–29. The “goddess of grass and grain” is probably either Demeter or Persephone—more likely the latter, if our poet had in mind Kleanthes’ play on the name Persephone as warm air (see OH 29.15–16n). The mention of winds is interesting. In Aristophanes’ account of the birth of Eros from an egg in the Birds, the egg is a wind-egg (line 695) and Eros is described as being like the swift whirlwinds (line 697). The choice of a wind-egg may just be a joke on Aristophanes’ part, playing off the incongruity of one thing being born out of another that is unproductive by nature. However, in at least one version of Orphic myth, the parents of Eros are Time and all the winds (Orphic fragment 360), and Sappho’s younger contemporary Alkaios said that Eros was the son of Iris (Rainbow) and Zephyros, the west wind (see OH 81i). A later poet, Antagoras of Rhodes (early third century BC) in a literary hymn to Eros frankly expresses his puzzlement as to the god’s parentage. He lists four possibilities: (1) Erebos and Night (alluding to Aristophanes’ comic account), (2) Aphrodite, (3) Earth, and (4) the winds. See further the discussion at West 1983, pp. 200–201. 5–7：与《俄耳甫斯颂歌》55.4–7 中阿佛洛狄忒的地理范围相比较；关于本集中此主题的其他地方，参见《俄耳甫斯颂歌》10.14–16 注释。提及冥界（“所有在塔尔塔罗斯中的”）或许意在唤起俄耳甫斯为带回心爱的欧律狄刻而下到冥界时，对哈迪斯和珀耳塞福涅施展魅惑的情景；参见《俄耳甫斯颂歌》87.9 注释，并比较奥维德《变形记》5.359–384 和 10.25–29。“草与谷物的女神”很可能指得墨忒耳或珀耳塞福涅——若诗人心中想到的是克莱安西斯对珀耳塞福涅名字作为暖空气的文字游戏（参见《俄耳甫斯颂歌》29.15–16 注释），则更可能是后者。提及风是耐人寻味的。在阿里斯托芬《鸟》中关于厄洛斯从蛋中诞生的描述里，那蛋是一个风蛋（第 695 行），而厄洛斯被描述为像迅疾的旋风（第 697 行）。选择风蛋可能只是阿里斯托芬的一个玩笑，利用了天生不育之物却生出另一事物的不协调性。 然而，在至少一个版本的俄耳甫斯神话中，厄洛斯的父母是时间与所有的风（俄耳甫斯残篇 360），而萨福的年轻同代人阿尔凯奥斯则说厄洛斯是彩虹女神伊里斯与西风神泽费罗斯的儿子（参见 OH 81i）。后来的诗人，罗德岛的安塔戈拉斯（公元前三世纪早期）在一首献给厄洛斯的文学颂诗中，坦率地表达了他对这位神祇出身的困惑。他列举了四种可能：（1）厄瑞玻斯与黑夜（暗指阿里斯托芬的喜剧叙述），（2）阿佛洛狄忒，（3）大地，以及（4）风。更多讨论可参见 West 1983, pp. 200–201。
59. To the Fates59. 致命运女神
The Fates (Greek Moirai) are three sisters who were thought to be responsible for certain immutable facts about the cosmos. Sometimes they are merged into the notion of a singular personified abstraction Fate. The word “moira” means “lot, portion.” When the early Greeks felt the need to explain why things happened to them the way they did, they cast their questions in terms of a personal “who is giving this” rather than an abstract “what is causing this,” and the Fates are an answer to the question of who is doing the giving; compare the concept of a daimōn (OH 73i). They thus represent what is allotted in life, the portion of life one receives. That this does not necessarily entail “preordained destiny” can be seen in the Iliad, where Akhilleus has a choice whether to return home, where he will live to a ripe old age but die unknown, or to return to battle, where he will die young but earn immortal glory (9.410–416). Euchenor, son of the seer Polyidos, had a somewhat similar choice: to stay home and die of sickness or to go to Troy and be killed by the Trojans (Iliad 13.663–670). In Plato’s “Myth of Er,” the souls about to be reborn are able to choose their next life, which is ratified by the Fates only after the choice is made (Republic 617d–621a). The idea that the Fates apportion destinies is a specific instance of the more general idea of apportioning limits on a cosmic level. The Fates also are the limits of the physical universe, and, since for the Greeks very often the physical structure of the world is also an ethical one, the Fates also delimit moral boundaries (see note to lines 8–10). In this connection, their role is sometimes expanded to being the protectors of these limits, punishing those who transgress the established boundaries, i.e., those who commit hubris. They are thus aligned with other divinities in our collection who are also concerned with maintenance of the cosmic order, such as Nemesis (OH 61), Justice (OH 63), Nomos (OH 64), and the Eumenides (OH 70). Most of all, though, they overlap with the Erinyes (OH 69), who in their hymn are actually called the Fates (translated “goddesses of fate” in line 16; see note).命运三女神（希腊语 Moirai）是三位姐妹，被认为掌管着宇宙中某些不可改变的事实。有时她们被融合成一个拟人化的抽象概念——命运。单词“moira”意为“份额、部分”。当早期希腊人感到需要解释为何事物会以特定方式发生时，他们用“谁在给予这个”而非抽象的“什么导致了这”来提出疑问，命运女神便是对“谁在给予”这一问题的回答；可对比精灵（daimōn）的概念（见《俄耳甫斯颂歌》73i 注释）。因此她们代表着生命中分配到的部分，即个人所获得的生命份额。这并不必然意味着“预先注定的宿命”，在《伊利亚特》中可见一斑：阿喀琉斯面临选择——是返回家乡安享天年却默默而终，还是重返战场英年早逝却赢得不朽荣耀（9.410–416）。预言家波吕伊多斯之子欧克诺尔也有类似选择：留在家中病逝，或前往特洛伊死于特洛伊人之手（《伊利亚特》13.663–670）。 在柏拉图的《厄尔神话》中，即将重生的灵魂能够选择自己的来世，而命运女神只会在选择完成后才予以确认（《理想国》617d–621a）。命运女神分配命运的观念，是宇宙层面分配界限这一更普遍观念的具体体现。命运女神也是物质宇宙的界限，并且，由于对希腊人而言，世界的物理结构往往也蕴含着伦理意义，命运女神同样划定了道德的边界（参见第 8-10 行注释）。在此关联下，她们的角色有时被扩展为这些界限的守护者，惩罚那些逾越既定边界的人，即那些犯下傲慢之罪者。因此，她们与我们文集中其他同样关注维护宇宙秩序的神祇结盟，例如涅墨西斯（OH 61）、正义女神（OH 63）、诺摩斯（OH 64）和欧墨尼得斯（OH 70）。然而，最重要的是，她们与厄里倪厄斯（OH 69）的职能有所重叠，后者在其颂歌中实际上被称为命运女神（第 16 行译为“命运女神”；参见注释）。
In Hesiod, the Fates are the daughters of Zeus and Themis (Theogony 904–906), and this relationship symbolically marks them as part of the divine order, just as it does with their sisters, the Seasons (see OH 43i). Of course, the divine order existed before Themis became a wife of Zeus, and Hesiod gives the alternate account that Night bore the Fates parthenogentically (Theogony 217–222; see also OH 61i). In this genealogy, the order they represent is an essential part of the development of the world. Orphic accounts also make the Fates the daughters of earlier generations. They are born from the “first gods” (Orphic fragment 176) or, along with the Hundred-Handers and the Kyklopes, are the children of Earth and Sky (Orphic fragment 82). The Kretan seer Epimenides makes them the daughters of Kronos and says their sisters are the Erinyes and Aphrodite (fragment 51). This last detail is interesting, not only because of the close relationship between the Erinyes and Fates already described but also in light of the fact that our hymn seems to be part of a grouping of divinities explicitly linked to Aphrodite (OH 55–60). We find the Fates and Aphrodite connected elsewhere. Pausanias reports an inscription he saw in Athens which claimed that Aphrodite was the oldest of the Fates (1.19.2).在赫西俄德笔下，命运女神是宙斯与忒弥斯的女儿（《神谱》904-906 行），这种亲缘关系象征性地将她们标记为神圣秩序的一部分，正如她们的姐妹时序女神亦是如此（参见 OH 43i 注）。当然，神圣秩序在忒弥斯成为宙斯妻子之前便已存在，赫西俄德另记载了倪克斯单性生育命运女神的说法（《神谱》217-222 行；另见 OH 61i 注）。在这一谱系中，她们所代表的秩序是世界发展的核心组成部分。俄耳甫斯教文献同样将命运女神归为更早世代的后裔——她们诞生于"初代神祇"（俄耳甫斯教残篇 176），或与百臂巨人、独眼巨人同为大地女神盖亚与天空之神乌拉诺斯的子女（俄耳甫斯教残篇 82）。克里特先知埃庇米尼得斯则称其为克洛诺斯之女，并指出其姐妹包括复仇三女神与阿佛洛狄忒（残篇 51）。最后这条记载尤为耐人寻味，不仅因为前文已述的复仇女神与命运女神间的紧密关联，更因本颂诗似乎隶属于一个明确与阿佛洛狄忒相关的神祇群组（OH 55-60）。命运女神与阿佛洛狄忒的关联在其他文献中亦有迹可循。 保萨尼亚斯记载了他在雅典看到的一处铭文，声称阿芙洛狄忒是命运三女神中最年长的一位（1.19.2）。
Our composer seems to have followed the Hesiodic version making Night the mother of the Fates. However, elsewhere in the collection, Night is called Kypris, another name of Aphrodite (see OH 3.2+n). This would further explain why the hymn to the Fates has been included among other figures connected with this goddess (see also OH 55i). Moreover, the “necessity” in line 18 of this hymn could possibly be understood as a personification. 3–4: The imagery used here is obscure. Those who dwell in caves near bodies of water are usually beings with definite chthonic connections, as, for example, the Erinyes in OH 69.3–4. Furthermore, the Fates themselves, called “daughters of Night” in line 1, are explicitly given chthonic coloring in this hymn. Here, however, it is clear that the location is celestial (see also OH 7.9n). The lake and the cave may have been imagined to be on Mount Olympos. Another possibility, though, is that the Fates are here being connected with the moon. This would certainly resolve the apparent contradiction, for the moon, while clearly a celestial body, nevertheless had strong chthonic ties. It was associated with Persephone, and indeed was sometimes thought to be the Isle of the Blest (for example, by Pythagoras; see Iamblichus Life of Pythagoras 82) or where souls went after death (see Plutarch De facie quae in orbe lunae apparet 942d–945d). The stars, too, could also be linked with souls (see OH 7.9n). In the lost poem Peplos (Robe), attributed to Orpheus, our source says that the Fates were allegorized as parts of the moon (with a wordplay here on the meaning of “moira,” “portion”). Furthermore, the Fates are said to be “clothed in white” insofar as they are parts of the moon’s light (Orphic fragment 407). It should be noted that the word here translated as “frozen” (Greek “leukos”) literally means “white,” a color that is sometimes used to describe moonlight. In the magical papyri, Moon is identified with the threads of the Fates (PGM 4.2795) and the singular being Fate (PGM 4.2861). It is true that celestial bodies were often thought to be composed of fire, but the moon was sometimes considered to be a mixture of fire and air—a view held by, among others, the Stoics (Plutarch De facie quae in orbe lunae apparet 921f), who thought that air froze water (Plutarch De primo frigido 949b–c)—and for Empedokles the moon was frozen air that had been separated from fire (Plutarch De facie quae in orbe lunae apparet 922c). In the manuscripts, the last line of this hymn reads: “This is the end of the song of the Fates, which Orpheus composed.” It is a dactylic hexameter line, the same meter used in all of the hymns in the collection. It is possible that it was part of the original composition, although it is difficult to see why only this hymn asserts its Orphic authorship. The explicit mention of Orpheus perhaps is meant to distinguish it from another hymn to the Fates, now lost to us, which was not by Orpheus (or even mistakenly attributed to him). On the other hand, it might be that this hymn was separate from the collection and was later added, due to its similarity to the other hymns; the line could have been part of the original and simply retained. Then again, it might simply be the work of a playful scribe engaging in a little poetic license. In this scenario, the line would have been a marginal note that eventually was misunderstood to have been part of the hymn and appended to its end. 60. To the Graces60. 致美惠三女神
The Graces (Greek Kharites) are a plurality of female divinities concerned with beauty, merriment, and good cheer. Aglaia is Splendor, Thalia Festivity, and Euphrosyne Joy, and their names are indicative of their function. They are frequently connected, and even confused, with the Seasons (see OH 43i). There is also some linguistic and conceptual overlap between this hymn and the one to the Seasons. Like the latter, the Graces are “ever-blooming,” the third one listed is “(thrice-)blessed,” flowers are used to describe their physical beauty, and both groups are called on to bring fertility. The affinity between these two groups is made even more concrete since the mother of the Graces is Eunomia, one of the Seasons. This differs from the Hesiodic account, where they are also daughters of Zeus, but their mother is Eurynome, one of the daughters of Okeanos (Theogony 907–911). The Orphic Rhapsodies, however, agree with our hymn (Orphic fragment 254). For other variations of their names and genealogy, see Pausanias 9.35.1–7. Of particular interest is his mention of mysteries that were performed near their statue at the entrance of the Athenian acropolis (9.35.3). Euripides recounts that they were sent by Zeus along with the Muses to mollify Kybele-Demeter, who was angry at the abduction of her daughter Persephone (Helen 1338–1345; see OH 27i). The Graces are especially associated with Aphrodite. In the Homeric Hymn to Aphrodite 5.60–64 they are the goddess’ attendants. In the Iliad Diomedes pierces Aphrodite’s robe, which was the handiwork of the Graces (5.337–338). Zeus orders Aphrodite to “pour grace around [Pandora’s] head,” and in the actual decking out of Pandora, the Graces themselves with the goddess Persuasion hang golden necklaces around her neck, while the Seasons crown her with a garland of spring flowers (Hesiod Works and Days 65 and 73–75). According to Pausanias, there was a sanctuary of the Graces at Elea where there were images of the goddesses—one holding a rose, another a die, the third a sprig of myrtle—and a statue of Eros next to them (6.24.6–7). Pausanias interprets this group by noting the symbolism of the rose and myrtle for Aphrodite and pointing out that young people, who are not yet marred by the ugliness of age, often play at dice.美惠三女神（希腊语 Kharites）是一组与美丽、欢乐和愉悦相关的女性神祇。阿格莱亚代表光辉，塔利亚象征庆典，欧佛洛绪涅则是喜悦，她们的名字揭示了各自的职能。她们常与季节女神（参见 OH 43i）相关联，甚至被混淆。本颂诗与献给季节女神的颂诗在语言和概念上存在一定重叠：与后者相似，美惠女神被描述为“永葆青春”，列于第三位的女神被称为“（三重）赐福者”，花朵被用来形容她们的形体之美，且两组神祇都被祈求赐予丰饶。由于美惠女神之母欧诺弥亚正是季节女神之一，这两组神祇的亲缘关系更为具体。这与赫西俄德的记载不同——在《神谱》（907-911 行）中她们虽同为宙斯之女，但其母为俄刻阿诺斯之女欧律诺墨。而《俄耳甫斯狂诗》的记载与本颂诗一致（俄耳甫斯残篇 254）。关于她们姓名与谱系的其他变体，可参阅保萨尼阿斯《希腊志》9.35.1-7。特别值得注意的是他提及在雅典卫城入口处她们雕像旁举行的秘仪（9.35.3）。 欧里庇得斯记述，她们与缪斯一同被宙斯派遣去安抚因女儿珀耳塞福涅被掳而愤怒的库柏勒-得墨忒耳（《海伦》1338–1345 行；参见《俄耳甫斯颂歌》27i）。美惠三女神尤其与阿佛洛狄忒相关联。在《荷马颂歌·致阿佛洛狄忒》5.60–64 中，她们是这位女神的侍从。在《伊利亚特》中，狄俄墨得斯刺穿了阿佛洛狄忒的长袍，那正是美惠三女神的杰作（5.337–338）。宙斯命令阿佛洛狄忒“将优雅倾注于[潘多拉]的头顶”，而在实际装扮潘多拉时，美惠三女神与劝说女神一起将金项链挂在她颈间，时序女神则用春花编成的花冠为她加冕（赫西俄德《工作与时日》65 行及 73–75 行）。据保萨尼阿斯记载，埃莱亚有一座美惠三女神的神殿，其中供奉着女神们的雕像——一位手持玫瑰，另一位拿着骰子，第三位握着一枝桃金娘——旁边还有一尊厄洛斯的雕像（6.24.6–7）。保萨尼阿斯解释这组雕像时指出，玫瑰和桃金娘象征着阿佛洛狄忒，并提到尚未被岁月丑陋所侵蚀的年轻人常以骰子为戏。
The Graces’ close association with Aphrodite helps to explain why their hymn follows on the heels of hymns dedicated to this goddess (OH 55) and to those explicitly connected with her: Adonis, Chthonic Hermes, and Eros (OH 56–58). For the connection of the Fates with Aphrodite, see OH 59i. The Fates and the Graces are further bound together by way of their mother Eunomia, whose name means “law-abiding.” As her daughters, the Graces are part of that divine order in which their mother partakes (see OH 43i) and that is exemplified by the Fates (see OH 59i) and those goddesses to whom the subsequent hymns are dedicated: Nemesis, Dike (another Season, and so one of their aunts!), Justice, and Nomos (OH 61–64).美惠三女神与阿芙洛狄忒的紧密联系，有助于解释为何她们的神颂紧随这位女神（《俄耳甫斯神颂》第 55 首）以及与她明确相关的神祇：阿多尼斯、冥界赫尔墨斯和厄洛斯（《俄耳甫斯神颂》第 56-58 首）的神颂之后。关于命运女神与阿芙洛狄忒的关联，参见《俄耳甫斯神颂》第 59 首注释。命运女神与美惠三女神通过她们的母亲欧诺弥亚进一步联系在一起，欧诺弥亚的名字意为“守法者”。作为她的女儿，美惠三女神属于其母亲所参与的神圣秩序的一部分（参见《俄耳甫斯神颂》第 43 首注释），这一秩序由命运女神（参见《俄耳甫斯神颂》第 59 首注释）以及后续神颂所献予的女神们所体现：涅墨西斯、狄刻（另一位时序女神，因此是她们的姑母之一！）、正义女神和诺摩斯（《俄耳甫斯神颂》第 61-64 首）。
61. Hymn to Nemesis61. 致涅墨西斯神颂
Nemesis is another personified abstraction that became deified. Her name comes from the verb “nemō,” “I deal out, distribute.” She is the goddess of righteous indignation, who punishes those who transgress customs and laws. Hesiod makes her the daughter of Night (born from no father) and describes her as a “woe for mortals” (Theogony 223–234). A more positive portrayal of this goddess appears in the conclusion to his account of the Iron Race of men. There is so much wickedness in the world that Nemesis apparently gives the human race up and leaves with Aidos (Shame) to Olympos (Works and Days 197–201). Both indignation and shame were important forces in early society that helped prevent unjust deeds and consequently contributed to constructing a stable community. Hesiod subtly links Nemesis and Dike in the Works and Days, since Dike, too, leaves the earth in the face of wicked acts; she rushes to her father, Zeus, to demand punishment against those who have mistreated her (Works and Days 256–262; see also OH 62i and OH 69.9n).涅墨西斯是另一个被神格化的拟人化抽象概念。她的名字源于动词"nemō"，意为"我分配、分发"。她是义愤女神，惩罚那些违反习俗与法律之人。赫西俄德将其描述为夜神之女（无父而生），并称她为"凡人的灾祸"（《神谱》223-234 行）。在描述人类铁器时代的结尾处，这位女神呈现出更积极的形象。当世间罪恶横行时，涅墨西斯显然放弃了人类，与艾多斯（羞耻之神）一同前往奥林匹斯山（《工作与时日》197-201 行）。在早期社会中，义愤与羞耻都是抑制不义行为、构建稳定社群的重要力量。赫西俄德在《工作与时日》中巧妙地将涅墨西斯与狄刻相联系——面对世间罪恶，狄刻同样离开了大地；她奔向父亲宙斯，要求惩罚那些虐待她的人（《工作与时日》256-262 行；另见 OH 62i 与 OH 69.9n 注释）。
Nemesis is connected with the Trojan War in an interesting variant. Zeus falls in love with her, but she flees his advances, out of shame and indignation (the words “aidos” and “nemesis” are used), since Zeus is her father. With the god in hot pursuit, she keeps changing herself into different animals, desperate to escape. Zeus catches up to her when she is in the form of a goose, and he mates with her in the form of a swan. Nemesis lays an egg, which is given to Leda, queen of Sparta, and out of the egg hatches Helen. The death and destruction that result in the war for her sake are thus connected with the righteous anger of Nemesis at the abuse of her father. For versions of this story, see Kypria fragment 7 (= Athenaios 8.334b–d), Apollodoros 3.10.7, and Pausanias 1.33.7; see also OH 79i. Other goddesses also become wrathful at such forced unions, e.g., Demeter at Poseidon (see OH 69i), and Persephone at Zeus (see OH 29i and OH 71.4–5+n).涅墨西斯与特洛伊战争的联系存在一个有趣的变体。宙斯爱上了她，但由于宙斯是她的父亲，涅墨西斯出于羞耻与愤慨（原文使用了“aidos”和“nemesis”这两个词）而躲避他的追求。在神祇的紧追不舍下，她不断将自己变成各种动物，绝望地试图逃脱。当她化身为一只鹅时，宙斯追上了她，并以天鹅的形态与她交合。涅墨西斯产下一枚蛋，这枚蛋被交给了斯巴达王后勒达，从蛋中孵出了海伦。因此，那场因她而起的战争所带来的死亡与毁灭，便与涅墨西斯对其父滥用权力的正当愤怒联系了起来。关于此故事的版本，可参阅《塞浦路亚》残篇 7（=阿特纳奥斯 8.334b–d）、阿波罗多洛斯 3.10.7 及保萨尼阿斯 1.33.7；另见《俄耳甫斯颂歌》79i。其他女神在面对此类强迫结合时也会变得愤怒，例如得墨忒耳对波塞冬（见《俄耳甫斯颂歌》69i），以及珀耳塞福涅对宙斯（见《俄耳甫斯颂歌》29i 及 71.4–5+n）。
This myth is reflected in the cult of Nemesis at Rhamnous, a town in Attika. Pausanias describes a statue by the famous sculptor Pheidias (modern scholars prefer to attribute it to his pupil Agorakritos) depicting Leda leading Helen to her mother Nemesis; also depicted is Leda’s husband, Tyndareus, with their children, as well as Agamemnon, Menelaos, Neoptolemos and Hermione, the daughter of Helen (1.33.8). The statue was built from marble that the Persians had arrogantly brought with them in their invasion of Attika, with the intent to build a trophy for the victory they felt inevitable; thus the goddess became explicitly connected with their defeat (Pausanias 1.33.2). The statue held an apple branch in its left hand and a libation bowl in its right (engraved with Ethiopians); on its head was a deer and images of Nike. The symbolism of Nike is clearly connected with the defeat of the Persians. The apple branch suggests fertility connections, maybe even a connection with Aphrodite, while the deer perhaps hints at Artemis or some other similar ancient mistress of animals; see Larson 2007, pp. 179–180. Themis had a shrine in Nemesis’ sanctuary (see OH 79i). Nemesis was also worshipped at Smyrna, where the abstraction becomes a plurality of three Nemeses (Pausanias 7.5.3).这一神话在阿提卡地区拉姆努斯镇的涅墨西斯崇拜中有所体现。保萨尼阿斯描述了一座由著名雕塑家菲迪亚斯（现代学者更倾向于将其归功于他的学生阿戈拉克里托斯）创作的雕像，描绘了勒达引领海伦走向其母涅墨西斯的情景；雕像中还刻画了勒达的丈夫廷达瑞俄斯及其子女，以及阿伽门农、墨涅拉俄斯、涅俄普托勒摩斯和海伦之女赫耳弥俄涅（1.33.8）。这座雕像采用波斯人入侵阿提卡时傲慢携带的大理石建造，原本他们意图用此石为自以为必然的胜利建立纪念碑；因而这位女神明确地与他们的败绩联系在一起（保萨尼阿斯 1.33.2）。雕像左手持苹果枝，右手持祭酒碗（碗上刻有埃塞俄比亚人形象）；头顶饰有鹿与尼刻女神像。尼刻的象征意义显然与波斯人的溃败相关。苹果枝暗示着丰饶的联系，甚至可能与阿佛洛狄忒相关，而鹿或许暗指阿耳忒弥斯或其他类似的古老动物女主人；参见拉森 2007 年著作第 179-180 页。忒弥斯在涅墨西斯的神殿中设有一座圣坛（参见《俄耳甫斯颂歌》79i）。 涅墨西斯在士麦那同样受到崇拜，在那里这一抽象概念演化为三位涅墨西斯女神（保萨尼阿斯 7.5.3）。
It is interesting that the Fates are placed before Nemesis in Hesiod’s list of Night’s progeny and that they are the ones who he says look over the deeds of mortals and gods and punish transgressions (Theogony 220–222). This is normally the purview of Nemesis. However, for the Greeks the ideas of justice and fate were intertwined in the cosmic order, so it is not surprising that at times divinities concerned with one of these should be concerned with the other as well (see OH 59i). Nemesis was sometimes called Adrasteia (Ineluctable) and invoked apotropaically before one would say something that could be construed as boasting or otherwise overbold (see, e.g., Aeschylus Prometheus Bound 936 and Plato Republic 451a). Adrasteia can function like Fate, too, and later is equated with Necessity; see West 1983, pp. 194–196. Nemesis became associated also with Tyche; compare lines 7–8 of the second century AD hymn to Nemesis by Mesomedes: “Beneath your wheel that neither ceases nor remains on the beaten track/there rolls the bright Tyche of men” and OH 72. Mesomedes further develops the idea of Nemesis as Fate through the image of scales (line 1, “O Nemesis, winged scales of life,” and line 13, “with scales in hand”) and the symbolism of measuring (line 11, “you measure out livelihood”; cf. Lakhesis the “allotter” at OH 59.16+n). This close relation probably influenced the placement of this hymn near the one dedicated to the Fates, and, insofar as Aphrodite is called “mother of Necessity” (OH 55.3), Nemesis could very well have been imagined as part of the Aphrodite block of hymns. The intimate bond between justice and the indignation that arises against those who transgress it further explains the grouping of this hymn with the three that follow it. The importance of acting in accordance to justice is thus emphasized. The first and last of the four (OH 64, to Nomos) are marked by their lack of offering, and it is likely that the initiates paused in their sacrifices and merely sang to these divinities. There is further a possible male/female pairing implied between Nemesis and Nomos (see OH 14.8–9n), whose names, incidentally, are etymologically related. The other two hymns sandwiched in between address the closely related pair of Dike and Justice. The themes of the blessings of justice and the inevitable punishment of the unjust unite all four and connect these figures with similar deities, namely, the Fates (OH 59), the Erinyes (OH 69), and the Eumenides (OH 70).值得注意的是，在赫西俄德所列的夜神后裔中，命运女神被置于涅墨西斯之前，且据他所言，正是命运女神监察着凡人与神祇的作为并惩罚越界行为（《神谱》220–222）。这本应是涅墨西斯的职责范畴。然而对古希腊人而言，正义与命运的理念在宇宙秩序中本就相互交织，因此涉及其中一方的神祇时常也会涉足另一方，这并不令人意外（参见《俄耳甫斯颂歌》59i）。涅墨西斯有时被称为阿德拉斯忒亚（意为"不可抗拒者"），人们会在可能被视为夸耀或过度狂妄的言论前呼唤其名以作禳解（例如参见埃斯库罗斯《被缚的普罗米修斯》936 及柏拉图《理想国》451a）。阿德拉斯忒亚亦可如命运般运作，后期更与必然性等同；参见韦斯特 1983 年著作第 194–196 页。涅墨西斯后来也与堤喀产生关联；试比较公元二世纪梅索梅德斯所作《涅墨西斯颂歌》第 7–8 行："在你这永不停歇亦不固守常轨的巨轮之下/翻滚着人类明灭不定的堤喀"，以及《俄耳甫斯颂歌》72。 梅索梅德斯通过天平的形象（第 1 行“哦，涅墨西斯，生命之翼的天平”和第 13 行“手持天平”）以及度量的象征（第 11 行“你分配生计”；参见《俄耳甫斯颂歌》59.16+注中“分配者”拉克西斯），进一步发展了涅墨西斯作为命运的观念。这种密切关系可能影响了这首颂歌被置于献给命运女神们的颂歌附近的位置，并且，鉴于阿佛洛狄忒被称为“必然之母”（《俄耳甫斯颂歌》55.3），涅墨西斯很可能被设想为阿佛洛狄忒颂歌组的一部分。正义与对违反正义者产生的义愤之间的紧密联系，进一步解释了这首颂歌与紧随其后的三首颂歌被归为一组。因此，依循正义行事的重要性得到了强调。这四首颂歌中的第一首和最后一首（《俄耳甫斯颂歌》64，致诺摩斯）以没有献祭为标志，很可能入会者在献祭时暂停，仅向这些神灵歌唱。此外，涅墨西斯与诺摩斯之间可能隐含着一对男女配对（参见《俄耳甫斯颂歌》14.8-9 注），而他们的名字在词源上恰好相关。 夹在中间的两首颂歌则献给了紧密相关的狄刻与正义这对神祇。正义的恩赐与对不义者必然的惩罚这一主题将四者统一起来，并将这些形象与类似的神祇联系起来，即命运三女神（OH 59）、厄里倪厄斯（OH 69）和欧墨尼得斯（OH 70）。
2 all-seeing eye: Similarly in line 8. A number of addressees in the collection are described in this way. The most relevant parallel is Dike (OH 62.1); see further OH 8.1n.2 全视之眼：第 8 行亦同。本诗集中多位受颂者皆以此方式描述。最相关的对应是狄刻（OH 62.1）；另见 OH 8.1 注释。
4: This line does not mean that Nemesis is herself inconsistent, arbitrary, or fickle. It is the wickedness of men that is so varied, and this entails that the principle embodied by Nemesis must appear differently in her various concrete manifestations. Compare the story of her flight from Zeus, where she is a shapeshifter. The line also fits in with the theme of deities who are multiform and ever-changing.4：此行并非意指涅墨西斯自身反复无常、任意妄为或变幻莫测。实乃人类之邪恶如此多变，这要求涅墨西斯所体现的原则在其各种具体显现中必然呈现不同面貌。可参照她逃离宙斯时化身千万的故事。此行亦契合诸神形态万千、变化不息的主题。
5: Fear as a motivation to act justly was recognized early on by the Greeks. An astounding witness to the fact is the fragment from the late fifth-century tragedy (or satyr play) Sisyphos, sometimes attributed to Euripides. In the fragment, the lead character baldly states that gods were invented merely as a means to frighten people into behaving themselves; cf. OH 69.15n.5：恐惧作为促使人们公正行事的动机，早在古希腊时期便已得到认可。公元前五世纪末的悲剧（或萨提尔剧）《西西弗斯》中的片段为此提供了惊人的佐证，该剧有时被归为欧里庇得斯所作。片段中，主角直言不讳地指出，神祇的创造仅仅是为了恐吓人们循规蹈矩；参见《俄耳甫斯颂歌》69.15 注。
6–7 the arrogant soul, / the reckless one: Transgression is properly a going beyond the bounds of what is allowed and/or appropriate, and the Greeks were very concerned about respecting boundaries and maintaining proper limits; see OH 63.7n and cf. OH 30i. This idea lies at the heart of the concept of hubris, a word not used in our hymn but found in Mesomedes’ (line 5: “hating destructive hubris of mortals”). See also OH 59.8–10+n.6–7 傲慢的灵魂，/ 鲁莽之人：僭越的本质在于逾越了被允许和/或适宜的界限，古希腊人极为重视对界限的尊重与适当限度的维持；参见《俄耳甫斯颂歌》63.7 注，并比较《俄耳甫斯颂歌》30i。这一观念构成了"hubris"（狂妄）概念的核心，该词虽未在本颂歌中出现，但见于梅索梅德斯的作品（第 5 行："憎恨凡人毁灭性的狂妄"）。另见《俄耳甫斯颂歌》59.8–10 及注。
8 you arbitrate all: Compare line 14 of Mesomedes’ hymn, where Nemesis is invoked as a judge, and the idea of Nemesis as Fate as noted in the introduction to this hymn.8 你裁决一切：比较梅索梅德斯颂歌第 14 行，其中涅墨西斯被呼求为审判者，以及本颂歌引言中提到的涅墨西斯即命运的观念。
62. To Dike62. 致狄刻
Dike (Right) is not really different from Justice in the next hymn, whose name in Greek (Dikaiosunē) is derived from Dike’s (see OH 63i). For Hesiod, she is one of the three Seasons and a daughter of Zeus and Themis (Theogony 901–903). She receives special attention in the Works and Days where she is represented as a maiden who takes vengeance on the unjust, particularly in juridical matters, whether she takes punishment into her own hands (220–224) or complains to her father, Zeus (256–262; see also OH 61i and OH 69.9n). Note that the word “dikē” in Greek can also mean “punishment.” Orphism adopts the Hesiodic genealogy (Orphic fragment 252) but adds a second one, making Dike the daughter of Nomos (Law; to whom OH 64 is addressed) and Eusebeia (Piety); see also OH 63i. Mesomedes in his hymn to Nemesis makes her the daughter of Dike; here genealogy reflects function. 63. To Justice63. 致正义
Justice (Dikaiosunē) was one of the most important, if not the most important, virtues in Greek ethical thought, often discussed by poets and philosophers. There is a certain amount of overlap between this word and “dikē,” and the two words may function as synonyms. One distinction between Dike and Justice in their portrayals here is that the former has a somewhat more concrete personalization while the latter is presented more as an abstract entity (but cf. OH 8.18, where Sun is called the “eye of justice,” and OH 62.1n). Justice also seems to be more broadly construed; see note to lines 14–15. We do find Justice personified and worshipped, although it is rare. Euripides is our earliest source for the personification. He mentions the “golden countenance of Justice” in his lost play Melanippe (fragment 486). An inscription on Delos from 115/114 BC identifies Isis with Justice as well as Tyche, Protogoneia (a feminine form of Protogonos, First-Born), Thalia (the name of one of the Graces that means “joy”), and Aphrodite the Righteous. Another inscription from Epidauros in the second century AD confirms that Justice received worship there. In Orphic theogony, Nomos (Law) and Eusebeia (Piety) are said to have given birth to Justice (Orphic fragment 248), and it is therefore notable that in the opening address to Mousaios both Justice and Piety are mentioned together (OH O.14). However, Hermias, the source for this genealogy, in the same work also says it is Dike who is their daughter. Whether he thought they were two distinct entities or he is using the names interchangeably is hard to determine. To make matters more complicated, Hermias again in the same work says that there are three Nights in Orphic mythology and that the third one gave birth to Justice (Orphic fragment 246). And another source says that, for Orpheus, Dike was a daughter of Zeus and Themis and that she was one of the Seasons (see OH 43i). These might represent different variants that developed independently over time and that are being indiscriminately used by later authors. However, as the multiple Nights show, it is possible that a single entity could be duplicated in Orphic mythopoetics. Clearly the notion of justice was as important to the Orphics as it was to the wider Greek world.正义（Dikaiosunē）是希腊伦理思想中最重要的美德之一，即便不是最核心的，也常被诗人与哲学家探讨。此词与“dikē”存在一定重叠，两者常可互换使用。在本书描绘中，Dike 与正义的一个区别在于，前者更具具体的人格化特征，而后者则更多呈现为抽象实体（但可参考《俄耳甫斯颂歌》8.18，其中太阳被称为“正义之眼”，以及 62.1 注释）。正义的概念似乎被更广泛地诠释；详见第 14-15 行注释。尽管罕见，我们确实发现正义被人格化并受到崇拜。欧里庇得斯是最早记载此人格化的文献来源，他在失传的剧作《墨拉尼珀》（残篇 486）中提及“正义的金色面容”。公元前 115/114 年提洛岛的一处铭文将伊西斯与正义、命运女神提喀、原初女神普罗托戈涅娅（原初之神普罗托戈诺斯的女性形态）、塔利亚（美惠三女神之一，意为“欢欣”）以及正直的阿佛洛狄忒等同。公元二世纪埃皮达鲁斯的另一处铭文证实，当地存在对正义的崇拜。 在俄耳甫斯神谱中，据说律法（Nomos）与虔敬（Eusebeia）生下了正义（俄耳甫斯残篇 248），因此值得注意的是，在对穆赛俄斯的开篇致辞中，正义与虔敬被一同提及（俄耳甫斯颂歌 O.14）。然而，提供这一谱系的赫尔米阿斯在同一著作中也称，正义是他们的女儿。他究竟认为这是两个不同的实体，还是在交替使用这些名称，这很难确定。更复杂的是，赫尔米阿斯在同一著作中再次提到，俄耳甫斯神话中有三位黑夜女神，而第三位生下了正义（俄耳甫斯残篇 246）。另一来源则称，对俄耳甫斯而言，正义是宙斯与忒弥斯的女儿，并且是时序女神之一（见俄耳甫斯颂歌 43i）。这些可能代表了随时间独立发展的不同变体，被后来的作者不加区分地使用。然而，正如多位黑夜女神所显示的，在俄耳甫斯的神话诗学中，单一实体被复制是可能的。显然，正义的概念对俄耳甫斯教派而言，与对整个希腊世界一样重要。
7 the balance of your mighty scales: Balance, equality, and fairness are important themes in this hymn; they also recur in the other three of the group. An important component in the Greek view of justice was that each person receives what they deserve; injustice occurs when the undeserving take more than their fair share (a form of hubris) and the deserving are short-changed. In section 29 of The Theology of Arithmetic (see OH 12.3n), the author says that the Pythagoreans considered the tetrad (i.e., the number four) to be Justice, because a square that had sides the length of four would have its area (length times width: 4 × 4 = 16) and its perimeter (four sides of 4 = 16) equal (Waterfield 1988, p. 63). 64. Hymn to Nomos64. 致法则的颂歌
This ends a sequence of four tightly integrated hymns. As with OH 61, there is no indication of incense, which suggests this was perhaps sung without being accompanied by any other ritual activity; together they mark the beginning and end of the series. A crescendo effect is achieved by the scope of each hymn. The first two, the hymns to Nemesis and Dike, are limited to the various races of men (cf. OH 61.2 and OH 62.3). The third hymn to Justice also is concerned with human justice, but at the very end expands to include all living creatures (OH 63.14–15+n). All three divinities are female, and their concern is with things that are alive. In this hymn, the male Nomos (Law) has been raised to a cosmic principle that sees to it that both the inanimate elements of nature and the creatures that live among them keep to their proper limits. This connects the hymn conceptually to the previous three, as respecting boundaries is a core component of Greek ethical thought (see OH 61.6–7n and OH 63.7n). The hymn is structured to reflect the cosmos-human duality. The first part expresses Nomos as the physical order of the universe (lines 1–4). A transitional bridge brings Nomos down to earth—literally (lines 5–6). The focus is then on Nomos as a foundational ethical force for living beings in general and the individual in particular (lines 7–11). This notion that the underlying structure of the cosmos is as ethical as it is physical and that this universal ethic is connected to moral action in the human sphere returns to a theme found in the earlier hymns (see OH 8.16n) and appears again near the end (see OH 86i); see also OH 59.8–10n and OH 69.15n.这标志着四首紧密相连的颂诗序列的结束。与《俄耳甫斯颂诗》第 61 首一样，此处未提及焚香仪式，暗示着这首颂诗或许是在没有其他仪式活动伴奏的情况下吟唱的；它们共同标志着这一系列颂诗的开端与终结。每首颂诗的视野范围营造出一种渐强的效果。前两首献给涅墨西斯和狄刻的颂诗，其范围仅限于人类的各个种族（参见《俄耳甫斯颂诗》61.2 和 62.3）。第三首献给正义的颂诗同样关注人类正义，但在结尾处扩展至涵盖所有生灵（《俄耳甫斯颂诗》63.14–15 及注释）。这三位神祇皆为女性，她们关切的是生命之物。而在这首颂诗中，男性的诺摩斯（法则）被提升为宇宙原则，确保自然界的无生命元素与栖居其间的生物皆恪守各自应有的界限。这在概念上将本颂诗与前三首联系起来，因为尊重边界是希腊伦理思想的核心组成部分（参见《俄耳甫斯颂诗》61.6–7 注释和 63.7 注释）。本颂诗的结构旨在体现宇宙与人类的二元性：第一部分将诺摩斯表述为宇宙的物理秩序（第 1–4 行）。 一座过渡性的桥梁将诺莫斯带至人间——字面意义上（第 5-6 行）。随后聚焦于诺莫斯作为普遍生命体及个体生存的根基性伦理力量（第 7-11 行）。这种认为宇宙深层结构兼具物理性与伦理性，且普世伦理与人类道德行为相连的观念，既呼应了早期颂诗中的主题（参见《俄耳甫斯颂诗》8.16 注释），又在临近结尾处重现（参见《俄耳甫斯颂诗》86i）；另见《俄耳甫斯颂诗》59。《俄耳甫斯颂诗》8.10 注释及《俄耳甫斯颂诗》69.15 注释。
The earliest evidence for the personification of Nomos is Pindar fragment 169a.1–4, which is cited by Plato (Gorgias 484b). Nomos as a divinity seems to have been appealing to the philosophers. A fragment of Herakleitos says that “all human laws [nomoi] are nourished by the one that is divine” (Kirk, Raven, and Schofield 1983, no. 250), which might imply that for him Nomos was a divinity. The Stoics, who were influenced greatly by Herakleitos, do explicitly recognize him as such. Philodemus tells us that the Stoic philosopher Khrysippos recognized “the sun, the moon, and the other stars as gods … as well as law (nomos)” (On Piety 11); compare lines 2–4 of this hymn. Philodemus also tells us that Khrysippos said Zeus was Nomos (On Piety 14). Kleanthes, an earlier Stoic philosopher, in his hymn to Zeus describes him as “steering everything with Nomos” (line 2); the same metaphor (albeit with different wording) is found in line 8 of this hymn. In Orphic thought, Nomos was also considered a god. He is the father to Dike and/or Justice (Orphic fragment 248; see OH 63i), and he sits next to the enthroned Zeus, who has Dike as a companion (Orphic fragment 247). This last idea is very similar to that expressed by Kleanthes.关于 Nomos 人格化的最早证据来自品达残篇 169a.1-4，该残篇被柏拉图引用（《高尔吉亚篇》484b）。Nomos 作为神祇似乎对哲学家们颇具吸引力。赫拉克利特的一个残篇提到“所有人类法律[nomoi]都受那神圣的一者滋养”（柯克、雷文与斯科菲尔德 1983 年编，编号 250），这可能暗示对他而言 Nomos 是一位神祇。深受赫拉克利特影响的斯多葛学派则明确承认其为神。斐洛德穆告诉我们，斯多葛哲学家克律西波斯承认“太阳、月亮及其他星辰为神……法律（nomos）亦为神”（《论虔敬》第 11 节）；可对照本颂诗第 2-4 行。斐洛德穆还记载克律西波斯称宙斯即为 Nomos（《论虔敬》第 14 节）。早期斯多葛哲学家克莱安西斯在其《宙斯颂》中描述宙斯“以 Nomos 统御万物”（第 2 行）；本颂诗第 8 行亦出现相同隐喻（尽管措辞不同）。在俄耳甫斯思想中，Nomos 同样被视为神祇。他是狄刻和/或正义之父（俄耳甫斯残篇 248；参见《俄耳甫斯颂诗》63i 注释），并端坐于御座的宙斯身侧——而宙斯以狄刻为伴（俄耳甫斯残篇 247）。 这一最后观点与克莱安西斯所表达的极为相似。

2–4: Compare this to Pan, who is conceived as the force that keeps the four elements separate (OH 11.13–18); see also OH 10.14–16n.2–4：将此与潘神相比较，他被构想为使四种元素保持分离的力量（《俄耳甫斯颂歌》11.13–18）；另见《俄耳甫斯颂歌》10.14–16 注释。

65. To Ares65. 致阿瑞斯
Ares, the god of war, is the son of Hera and Zeus (Hesiod Theogony 921–923). Although Athene is also concerned with war (see OH 32i), she represents the strategic, intellectual side, while Ares portrays the blood-and-guts aspect. In literature, the two are sometimes brought together in sharp contrast. They fight against each other in epic poetry, whether directly (Iliad 21.391–414) or through a heroic proxy. Athene gives direct assistance to Diomedes when he attacks Ares (Iliad 5.755–863), and she helps Herakles in his battle against Kyknos (the son of Ares) and Ares himself (Hesiod Shield 433–466). Athene employs reason in trying to restrain Ares’ anger at the death of one of his mortal sons on two occasions, further emphasizing the gulf between intelligence and pure battle rage (Iliad 15.100–142 and Hesiod Shield 446–449). The ancient Greeks in general had a strong distaste for the violence of war, and the negative treatment of Ares in myth is a reflection of this. The sons of Aloeus, Otos and Ephialtes, capture him, place him in chains, and keep him in a cauldron for thirteen months; Hermes eventually has to rescue him (Iliad 5.385–391). Zeus himself harshly rebukes him when he returns to Olympos fresh after being wounded by Diomedes (Iliad 5.888–898). Ares is often associated with aggressive figures who are threats to civilization, such as the Amazons. However, there is a positive side to Ares as well. In the Iliad, being called a “servant of Ares” (2.110), a “scion of Ares” (2.540), and the like is a mark of approval and praise. Ares is also a figure of masculine beauty; for example, Sappho praises a bridegroom as being as handsome as Ares (fragment 111). When the gods sing and dance, Ares also takes part (Homeric Hymn to Apollon 3.186–206). The ambiguity of his position in the Greek pantheon may be seen symbolically in his children with Aphrodite (Hesiod Theogony 933–937). Their two sons are Fear and Panic. They are often portrayed as driving the chariot of their father, and they rescue him from Herakles after Kyknos is slain. Their daughter, on the other hand, is Harmonia, the embodiment of civil concord (see also OH 55i). The legendary foundation of Thebes also reflects Ares’ ambiguity. Kadmos slays a dragon who is either an offspring or favorite of Ares. The teeth of the dragon are sown, and immediately armed warriors sprout out of the earth and commence fighting. Only five survive the savage fray, and these five become the forefathers of the five noble houses of Thebes. After this, though, Kadmos marries Ares’ daughter Harmonia, and the city is founded. Cults involving Ares are few; see Larson 2007, pp. 156–157, for details. Another war god, Enyalios, who interestingly had a female counterpart named Enyo, was eventually merged with Ares, although traces of independent cult still survived; see OH 76i.战神阿瑞斯是赫拉与宙斯之子（赫西俄德《神谱》921–923）。尽管雅典娜同样司掌战争（参见《俄耳甫斯颂歌》32i），但她代表的是战略与智谋层面，而阿瑞斯则象征着血腥残暴的厮杀。在文学作品中，二者常被置于鲜明对比之中。史诗中他们或直接对抗（《伊利亚特》21.391–414），或通过英雄代理人交锋：雅典娜曾直接协助狄俄墨得斯攻击阿瑞斯（《伊利亚特》5.755–863），并帮助赫拉克勒斯对抗库克诺斯（阿瑞斯之子）及阿瑞斯本尊（赫西俄德《赫拉克勒斯之盾》433–466）。雅典娜曾两度运用理性试图平息阿瑞斯因其凡人子嗣之死燃起的怒火，进一步凸显了智慧与纯粹战怒之间的鸿沟（《伊利亚特》15.100–142 与赫西俄德《赫拉克勒斯之盾》446–449）。古希腊人普遍对战争暴力怀有强烈厌恶，神话中对阿瑞斯的负面刻画正是这种观念的映照——阿罗欧斯之子奥托斯与厄菲阿尔忒斯曾擒获阿瑞斯，将其锁链加身囚于铜釜中长达十三个月，最终不得不由赫尔墨斯出手相救（《伊利亚特》5.385–391）。 宙斯本人曾严厉斥责他，当他在被狄俄墨得斯（《伊利亚特》5.888–898）刺伤后，刚刚返回奥林匹斯山时。阿瑞斯常与威胁文明的侵略性人物联系在一起，例如亚马逊人。然而，阿瑞斯也有积极的一面。在《伊利亚特》中，被称为“阿瑞斯的仆人”（2.110）、“阿瑞斯的后裔”（2.540）等，是一种认可和赞扬的标志。阿瑞斯也是男性美的象征；例如，萨福赞美一位新郎像阿瑞斯一样英俊（片段 111）。当众神歌唱和舞蹈时，阿瑞斯也参与其中（《荷马颂歌·阿波罗》3.186–206）。他在希腊万神殿中地位的模糊性，可能象征性地体现在他与阿佛洛狄忒所生的子女身上（赫西俄德《神谱》933–937）。他们的两个儿子是恐惧和恐慌。他们常被描绘为驾驶父亲的战车，并在库克诺斯被杀后从赫拉克勒斯手中救出他。而他们的女儿则是和谐女神哈耳摩尼亚，她是公民和谐的化身（另见 OH 55i）。底比斯的传奇建立也反映了阿瑞斯的矛盾性。卡德摩斯杀死了一条龙，这条龙要么是阿瑞斯的后代，要么是他的宠儿。 龙牙被播下，武装战士即刻从大地中破土而出，展开厮杀。仅有五人在残酷的搏斗中幸存，这五人成为底比斯五大贵族世家的始祖。此后，卡德摩斯迎娶战神阿瑞斯之女哈耳摩尼亚，城市由此建立。涉及阿瑞斯的崇拜仪式寥寥无几；详见拉森 2007 年著作第 156-157 页。另一位战神厄倪阿利俄斯——有趣的是他有一位名为厄倪俄的女性对应神祇——最终与阿瑞斯融合，尽管独立的崇拜痕迹依然留存；参见《俄耳甫斯颂歌》第 76 首注疏。
As Ares is a god who controls war, he also can perforce control peace in the sense that he can prevent war from breaking out in the world (compare line 6). Our hymn is divided into two parts that clearly play on these two sides. The violent and bloody nature of the god is given adequate expression in the first five lines; the hymn does not shirk from admitting this aspect of the god. Yet he is asked to transform himself into an agent of peace in the final four lines. This follows the pattern found in many of the other hymns in the collection: a divinity who has the potential to wreak great harm is asked propitiously to manifest themselves in their beneficial guise. This hymn should be read in conjunction with the Homeric Hymn to Ares, which most likely dates from the Hellenistic period or later, possibly even composed by Proclus; see West 1970. For the placement of this hymn with the following one to Hephaistos, compare line 10 of the address to Mousaios. After the digression from the hymn to Aphrodite to four abstractions concerned with order and law (OH 61–64), we return to two major Olympian deities who are both sons of Zeus and who both have associations with Aphrodite. The relationship between peace and justice connects this particular hymn with the previous four and eases the transition.既然阿瑞斯是掌控战争的神祇，他自然也能够在某种意义上掌控和平——即阻止世间战火燃起的能力（对照第六行）。我们的颂歌分为两个部分，清晰地展现了这两种面向。前五行充分表达了这位神祇暴烈嗜血的本性；颂歌并未回避神的这一面。然而在最后四行中，他被祈求转化为和平的使者。这遵循了本诗集中许多其他颂歌的模式：一位可能造成巨大伤害的神祇被恳切地祈求以仁慈的形象显现。此颂歌应与《荷马颂歌·致阿瑞斯》对照阅读，后者很可能创作于希腊化时期或更晚，甚至可能出自普罗克洛斯之手；参见韦斯特 1970 年的研究。关于此颂歌与后续赫菲斯托斯颂歌的编排，可对照致穆赛俄斯的第十行。在从阿佛洛狄忒颂歌转向四个关乎秩序与法则的抽象概念（《俄耳甫斯颂歌》61-64）的插叙之后，我们重新回到两位重要的奥林匹亚神祇——他们都是宙斯之子，且都与阿佛洛狄忒存在关联。和平与正义的关系将这首特定的颂歌与前四首联系起来，并缓和了过渡。
5 rude clash: The word for rude, “amouson,” literally means “without the Muses.” The activities of these goddesses are intricately bound up with peace (see OH 76i), although Ares, as mentioned in the introduction to this hymn, is not unfamiliar with their charms. The opposition between war and the arts is powerfully portrayed by Homer when he shows us the great warrior Akhilleus, who in anger has withdrawn from the fighting at Troy, in his tent, singing the deeds of the great men of the past (Iliad 9.185–194). In the Greek text, this word significantly is the last one before the composer asks Ares to leave off from his war-like nature in the following line.5 粗鲁的冲突：粗鲁一词“amouson”字面意思是“没有缪斯”。这些女神的活动与和平紧密相连（见 OH 76i），尽管如本颂歌引言所述，阿瑞斯对她们的魅力并不陌生。荷马有力地描绘了战争与艺术的对立，他向我们展示了伟大的战士阿喀琉斯，他在愤怒中从特洛伊的战斗中退出，在帐篷里歌唱过去伟人的事迹（《伊利亚特》9.185–194）。在希腊文本中，这个词在作曲家要求阿瑞斯在下一行放弃其好战本性之前，具有重要的意义。
7 Kypris: Another name for Aphrodite (see OH 22.7+n). Ares is often portrayed as a lover of Aphrodite, as in the somewhat risqué story of how Hephaistos captures the adulterous pair in flagrante, sung by the bard Demodokos as part of the entertainment for Odysseus at Scheria; see OH 66i. There seems to have been an Orphic version of their relationship in which Ares rapes Aphrodite (Orphic fragment 275). In one fragment from the Shorter Krater, a work attributed to Orpheus, the gods are interpreted allegorically, and Ares, who is equivalent to war, is explicitly contrasted with Aphrodite, who is made equivalent to peace (Orphic fragment 413.4).7 库普里斯：阿佛洛狄忒的别名（参见 OH 22.7+注）。阿瑞斯常被描绘为阿佛洛狄忒的情人，如在吟游诗人德摩多科斯为奥德修斯在斯刻里亚岛娱乐时所唱的略带情色意味的故事中，赫菲斯托斯当场捉奸这对通奸者；参见 OH 66 注。似乎存在一个俄耳甫斯版本的关于他们关系的传说，其中阿瑞斯强奸了阿佛洛狄忒（俄耳甫斯残篇 275）。在《短篇克拉特》——一部归于俄耳甫斯名下的作品——的一个残篇中，诸神被寓言式地解释，阿瑞斯等同于战争，与阿佛洛狄忒（等同于和平）形成鲜明对比（俄耳甫斯残篇 413.4）。
